items.q: A 68-year-old man suffering from recurrent angina underwent a coronary angiogram. It reveals 90% stenosis of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Based on this finding, which portion of the heart is most likely susceptible to ischemic damage?
o: Anterior two thirds of interventricular septum
Posterior one third of interventricular septum
items.w: The LAD (anterior interventricular artery) is one of the two terminal branches of the short left main coronary artery. It runs in the anterior interventricular groove with the great cardiac vein, so the muscle it feeds lies on the front of the heart: the sternocostal surface of both ventricles, the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum and the A-V bundle. A 90% LAD stenosis therefore puts the anterior septum at risk. The posterior third of the septum and the diaphragmatic surface depend on the posterior interventricular artery instead. (Anatomy L4 slides, in-class case)

x.1: The posterior 1/3 of the septum is supplied by the posterior interventricular (descending) artery, not the LAD.
x.2: The artery to the AV node comes from the RCA (80%) or the circumflex (20%), not the LAD.
x.3: The diaphragmatic surface of both ventricles is supplied by the posterior interventricular artery (and in co-dominance a circumflex branch).
x.4: The right atrium gets atrial branches of the right coronary artery.

m.1: mixes up LAD and PDA septal territory
m.2: thinks LAD supplies the AV node
m.3: mixes up sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces

items.q: A client's angiogram shows a blocked posterior interventricular (descending) artery. Which region should the nurse anticipate is at greatest risk of ischemia?
o: Posterior one third of the interventricular septum
Anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum
items.w: The posterior interventricular (descending) artery runs in the posterior interventricular groove together with the middle cardiac vein. It supplies the diaphragmatic surface of both ventricles and the posterior one third of the interventricular septum. The septum is therefore shared: the front two thirds belong to the LAD and the back third to the PDA, so a PDA block threatens the posterior septum. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: The anterior 2/3 of the septum is LAD territory.
x.2: The sternocostal surface of both ventricles is supplied by the LAD.
x.3: The left atrium receives branches of the circumflex artery.
x.4: The infundibulum is supplied by the right conus artery, an early RCA branch.

m.1: mixes up LAD and PDA septal territory
m.2: mixes up sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces

items.q: A client has a sudden occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery. Which structures should the nurse recognize may lose their arterial supply? Select all that apply.
o: Right ventricle via the acute (right) marginal branch
Posterior one third of the interventricular septum
Anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum
Left ventricle via the obtuse (left) marginal branch
items.w: The RCA arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the coronary groove, first between the right atrium and right ventricle and then posteriorly. Along the way it gives the artery to the SA node (65% of people), the artery to the AV node (80%), ventricular branches and the acute (right) marginal artery to the right ventricle, and it ends as the posterior interventricular artery that supplies the posterior third of the septum. A proximal occlusion can therefore starve all of these. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.4: The anterior 2/3 of the septum is supplied by the LAD.
x.5: The obtuse (left) marginal artery is a branch of the circumflex, a branch of the left coronary.

m.4: thinks RCA supplies the anterior septum
m.5: mixes up acute and obtuse marginal

items.q: A client with angina asks where the coronary arteries begin. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
o: The right coronary artery arises from the right aortic sinus, just above the right cusp of the aortic valve.
The right coronary artery arises from the posterior aortic sinus.
The left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary trunk.
Both coronary arteries arise from the arch of the aorta.
items.w: The ascending aorta has three sinuses just above the cusps of the aortic valve: right, left and posterior. The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus and the left coronary artery from the left (anterior) aortic sinus. The posterior sinus gives no coronary branch. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: The posterior aortic sinus lies above the posterior cusp and gives no coronary artery.
x.2: The left coronary artery only runs between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle; it arises from the left aortic sinus.
x.3: The arch gives the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; the coronaries arise from sinuses of the ascending aorta.

m.1: thinks a coronary arises from the posterior sinus
m.2: confuses the LCA's course with its origin

items.q: A client develops complete heart block after a coronary occlusion. The nurse knows the artery to the AV node most often arises from which vessel?
items.w: The AV node sits in the conduction path between atria and ventricles, so losing its blood supply can block conduction. The artery to the AV node comes from the right coronary artery in about 80% of people and from the circumflex in about 20%. The LAD supplies the A-V bundle further down the conducting system. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: The circumflex gives the artery to the AV node in only about 20% of people.
x.2: The LAD supplies the A-V bundle, not the AV node itself.
x.3: The obtuse marginal is a circumflex branch to the left ventricle.

m.1: reverses the AV-node percentages
m.2: thinks LAD supplies the AV node

items.q: A nursing student describes the blood supply of the SA node. Which statement by the student is accurate?
o: It arises from the right coronary artery in about 65% of people and from the circumflex in about 35%.
It arises from the circumflex in about 65% of people and from the right coronary in about 35%.
It always arises from the left anterior descending artery.
It arises from the right conus artery.
items.w: The SA node artery is a branch of the right coronary artery in about 65% of people and of the circumflex branch of the left coronary in about 35%. Knowing the percentages helps predict which occlusion can disturb the pacemaker. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: The percentages are reversed: the RCA supplies the SA node in about 65%.
x.2: The LAD supplies the sternocostal surface, anterior 2/3 of the septum and the A-V bundle, not the SA node.
x.3: The right conus artery goes to the infundibulum of the right ventricle.

m.1: reverses the SA-node percentages

items.q: A nurse states that the LAD supplies the A-V bundle as well as the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum.
items.w: The anterior interventricular artery (LAD) supplies the sternocostal surface of both ventricles, the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the A-V bundle. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: This statement is true: the A-V bundle is listed among the LAD's territories.

items.q: A client's angiography report reads "left dominant circulation." Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?
o: The posterior interventricular artery is a large branch of the circumflex artery.
The posterior interventricular artery is a large branch of the right coronary artery.
The RCA gives the posterior interventricular branch and the circumflex sends a branch to the diaphragmatic left ventricle.
The circumflex supplies the SA node in every client.
items.w: Dominance is named by which artery gives the posterior interventricular artery. In left dominance (15% on the slide) the posterior interventricular artery is a large branch of the circumflex; in right dominance (15%) it is a large branch of the right coronary; in co-dominance (70%) the RCA gives it and the circumflex also reaches the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle. Note: the slide gives co-dominance as the most common pattern (70%); many textbooks give right dominance as the most common instead, so check which figure your instructor expects. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: That describes right dominance.
x.2: That describes co-dominance (balanced circulation).
x.3: The circumflex supplies the SA node in only about 35% of people, whatever the dominance.

m.1: mixes up right and left dominance
m.2: mixes up co-dominance and left dominance

items.q: While reviewing a cardiac venogram with a client, the nurse identifies where each vein runs or ends. Match each vein to its location.

choices: Anterior interventricular groove, with the LAD
Posterior interventricular groove, with the posterior interventricular artery
Posterior wall of the right atrium
Anterior wall of the right atrium

items.w: The heart drains by three routes. Most blood collects into the coronary sinus, which lies between the left atrium and the diaphragmatic surface and ends in the posterior wall of the right atrium; its tributaries include the great cardiac vein (with the LAD in the anterior groove) and the middle cardiac vein (with the PDA in the posterior groove). The 2-3 anterior cardiac veins of the right ventricle end in the anterior wall of the right atrium, and the venae cordis minimi open directly into the chambers. Note: one slide says 3-4 anterior cardiac veins and another says 2-3. (Anatomy L4 slides, slide exercise)

x.4: This is how the venae cordis minimi drain, not any of the named veins.

m.4: confuses named veins with venae cordis minimi

rs.0: During cardiac surgery the nurse watches the surgeon trace the vein that accompanies the LAD. In which location does the great cardiac vein run?
rs.1: A client's venogram highlights the middle cardiac vein. Where should the nurse expect this vein to run?
rs.2: A nurse explains to a client where the heart's main venous channel empties. Where does the coronary sinus end?
rs.3: A nurse reviews the small veins draining the right ventricle. Where do the anterior cardiac veins end?

items.q: A nurse explains to a client that the coronary sinus empties into the posterior wall of the left atrium.
items.w: False. The coronary sinus lies between the left atrium and the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, but it terminates in the posterior wall of the RIGHT atrium, like the rest of the systemic venous return. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.0: The coronary sinus ends in the right atrium, not the left.

m.0: thinks coronary sinus drains into left atrium

items.q: A client's coronary sinus is being cannulated for a procedure. Which veins should the nurse recognize as tributaries that drain into it? Select all that apply.
o: Oblique vein of the left atrium
items.w: The coronary sinus collects five tributaries: the great, middle and small cardiac veins, the posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium. The anterior cardiac veins and the venae cordis minimi do not join it; they drain straight into the right atrium or the chambers. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.4: Anterior cardiac veins bypass the coronary sinus and end directly in the anterior wall of the right atrium.
x.5: Venae cordis minimi drain directly into the cardiac chambers.

m.4: thinks anterior cardiac veins join the coronary sinus

items.q: Before a cardiac exam, a nurse marks the outline of a client's heart on the chest wall. Point A lies at the lower border of the left {1} costal cartilage, point B at the upper border of the right {2} costal cartilage, and point D, the apex, lies in the left {3}, 3.5 inches from the midline.
items.w: Four points outline the heart: A (lower border of the left 2nd costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum), B (upper border of the right 3rd costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum), C (right 6th costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum) and D (left 5th intercostal space, 3.5 inches from the midline). Joining them gives the borders: upper A-B, right B-C, lower C-D and left D-A. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.0:1: The left 3rd costal cartilage is where the pulmonary valve lies, not point A.
x.0:2: The left 4th costal cartilage marks the mitral valve.
x.1:1: The 2nd costal cartilage is point A on the LEFT side.
x.1:2: The right 6th costal cartilage is point C, the lower end of the right border.
x.2:1: The left 4th intercostal space marks the tricuspid valve.
x.2:2: The 6th costal cartilage is point C, on the right.

m.0:1: puts point A one level too low
m.1:1: swaps the levels of points A and B
m.2:1: places the apex one space too high

items.q: A nurse is marking the right border of a client's heart on the chest wall. Between which two points should the line be drawn?
o: From the right 3rd costal cartilage (B) to the right 6th costal cartilage (C)
From the left 2nd costal cartilage (A) to the right 3rd costal cartilage (B)
From the right 6th costal cartilage (C) to the left 5th intercostal space (D)
From the left 5th intercostal space (D) to the left 2nd costal cartilage (A)
From the left 3rd costal cartilage to point C
items.w: The borders are named by joining the four surface points in order: upper border A-B, right border B-C, lower border C-D and left border D-A. The right border therefore runs from the upper border of the right 3rd costal cartilage down to the right 6th costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum. The coronary groove is a separate line from the left 3rd costal cartilage to point C. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: A-B is the upper border.
x.2: C-D is the lower border.
x.3: D-A is the left border.
x.4: This line marks the coronary groove, not a border.

m.1: mixes up upper and right borders

items.q: A nurse places the stethoscope to locate the surface marking of a client's mitral valve. Where is the mitral valve located?
o: Opposite the left 4th costal cartilage, behind the left half of the sternum
Behind the left 3rd costal cartilage at its junction with the sternum
Opposite the left 3rd intercostal space, behind the left margin of the sternum
Opposite the left 4th intercostal space, behind the midline of the sternum
Left 5th intercostal space, 3.5 inches from the midline
items.w: The valves lie in a diagonal line behind the sternum, from high on the left to low in the middle, remembered as PAMT. Pulmonary: behind the left 3rd costal cartilage at its junction with the sternum. Aortic: opposite the left 3rd intercostal space. Mitral: opposite the left 4th costal cartilage behind the left half of the sternum. Tricuspid: opposite the left 4th intercostal space behind the midline of the sternum. (Anatomy L4 slides)

x.1: That is the surface marking of the pulmonary valve.
x.2: That is the surface marking of the aortic valve.
x.3: That is the surface marking of the tricuspid valve.
x.4: That is point D, the apex of the heart, not a valve.

m.1: mixes up mitral and pulmonary valve markings
m.2: mixes up mitral and aortic valve markings
m.3: mixes up mitral and tricuspid valve markings

items.q: A nurse reviews the surface markings of the heart valves. Arrange the valves from the highest to the lowest position on the chest wall.
items.w: The mnemonic PAMT gives the order from top to bottom: pulmonary behind the left 3rd costal cartilage, aortic opposite the left 3rd intercostal space, mitral opposite the left 4th costal cartilage and tricuspid opposite the left 4th intercostal space. Each valve sits about half a level lower than the one before. (Anatomy L4 slides)

items.q: A client is scheduled for percutaneous coronary intervention. Arrange the steps of the procedure in the order they occur.
o: A catheter is passed retrograde from the radial or femoral artery
The catheter reaches the ascending aorta
Contrast is injected into the orifice of each coronary artery and photographed
A stent is placed to open the narrowed vessel
items.w: With the client under local anesthesia, a catheter is passed retrograde from the radial or femoral artery directly into the ascending aorta, where the coronary arteries begin. Multiple small doses of radiopaque contrast are injected into the orifice of each coronary artery to photograph every segment. A stent may then be placed to open a vessel narrowed by atherosclerotic plaque. (Anatomy L4 slides)

items.q: A 45-year-old man is in surgery. While seated at the head of the operating table, the anesthesiologist periodically checks the patient's pulse by palpating the artery located anterior to the tragus of the external ear. Which of the following arteries is being utilized to monitor the patient's pulse?
items.w: The external carotid artery ends inside the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries. The superficial temporal artery then ascends just in front of the tragus of the ear, where it can be felt, which makes it a convenient pulse for the anesthesiologist at the head of the table. (Anatomy L5 slides, in-class case)

x.1: The maxillary artery is the other terminal branch of the external carotid; it runs deep, not in front of the tragus.
x.2: The posterior auricular artery is an external carotid branch that runs behind the ear.
x.3: The facial artery is an external carotid branch to the face, not in front of the tragus.
x.4: The internal carotid has no branches in the neck and enters the skull through the carotid canal.

m.1: mixes up the two terminal ECA branches

items.q: A nurse palpates the carotid pulse and recalls where the common carotid artery divides. At which level does the common carotid artery end?
o: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4)
At the outer border of the first rib
Behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland
items.w: The common carotid arteries arise differently on each side (right from the brachiocephalic artery behind the sternoclavicular joint, left from the arch of the aorta), ascend inside the carotid sheath and end at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, between C3 and C4, by dividing into the external and internal carotid arteries. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.1: That is where the right common carotid begins from the brachiocephalic artery.
x.2: That is where the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery.
x.3: That is where the external carotid ends.
x.4: That is where the internal jugular vein begins.

m.1: confuses origin with termination
m.3: confuses common and external carotid termination

items.q: Before an internal jugular cannulation, the nurse reviews the relations of the common carotid artery in the carotid sheath. Which structure lies lateral to the artery?
items.w: Inside the carotid sheath the common carotid artery is related medially to the trachea and larynx and laterally to the internal jugular vein. Knowing that the vein is lateral helps the operator avoid the artery during a jugular puncture. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.1: The trachea lies medial to the common carotid artery.
x.2: The larynx lies medial to the common carotid artery.
x.3: Scalenus anterior is a relation of the subclavian artery, which it divides into three parts.

m.1: reverses medial and lateral relations
m.2: reverses medial and lateral relations

items.q: A client needs ligation of the external carotid artery. Which arteries should the nurse recognize arise directly from it? Select all that apply.
items.w: The external carotid gives eight branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital and posterior auricular, then ends as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. The inferior thyroid, transverse cervical and vertebral arteries all come from the subclavian system instead. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.4: The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.
x.5: The vertebral artery is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.
x.6: The transverse cervical artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk.

m.4: mixes up superior and inferior thyroid origins

items.q: A nurse teaching about cerebral blood supply states that the internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck.
items.w: True. The internal carotid artery arises at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, gives no branches in the neck, enters the cranial cavity through the carotid canal and supplies the brain, eyes, forehead and part of the nose. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.1: This statement is true: the internal carotid has no branches in the neck.

items.q: A client is being assessed for compression of the subclavian artery in the root of the neck. Which structure divides this artery into three parts?
o: Scalenus anterior, which passes anterior to the artery
Sternomastoid, which the external jugular vein crosses
The outer border of the first rib
The upper border of the thyroid cartilage
items.w: The subclavian artery arches laterally in the root of the neck and ends at the outer border of the first rib as the axillary artery. Scalenus anterior passes in front of it and divides it into three parts: the first part medial to the muscle, the second behind it and the third lateral to it. Each part has its own branches. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.1: The sternomastoid is the muscle the external jugular vein descends over.
x.2: The outer border of the first rib is where the subclavian ends and becomes the axillary artery.
x.3: That level marks the end of the common carotid artery.

m.1: confuses neck muscles
m.2: confuses termination with the dividing muscle

items.q: A nurse reviews the branches of the subclavian artery before a neck procedure. Match each artery to the part of the subclavian artery it arises from.
items.w: Scalenus anterior divides the subclavian artery into three parts. The first part (medial) gives the vertebral artery, the internal thoracic artery and the thyrocervical trunk. The second part (behind the muscle) gives the costocervical trunk, which divides into the superior intercostal and deep cervical arteries. The third part (lateral) gives the dorsal scapular artery in about 66% of people. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.3: The external carotid gives neck branches like the superior thyroid but none of these.

m.3: mixes subclavian and carotid branches

rs.0: A client has a vertebral artery injury. From which part of the subclavian artery does the vertebral artery arise?
rs.1: A nurse traces the costocervical trunk on a client's angiogram. Which part of the subclavian artery gives this trunk?
rs.2: A nurse reviews a client's shoulder angiogram showing the dorsal scapular artery. Which part of the subclavian artery gives it?
rs.3: A client is being evaluated for an internal thoracic artery graft. Which part of the subclavian artery gives the internal thoracic artery?

items.q: A client is undergoing thyroid surgery near the thyrocervical trunk. Which arteries should the nurse recognize as branches of this trunk? Select all that apply.
items.w: The thyrocervical trunk is one of the three branches of the first part of the subclavian artery. It gives the inferior thyroid, transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries. The costocervical trunk from the second part gives the superior intercostal and deep cervical arteries. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.3: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid.
x.4: The deep cervical artery is a branch of the costocervical trunk (2nd part).
x.5: The superior intercostal artery is a branch of the costocervical trunk (2nd part).

m.3: mixes up superior and inferior thyroid origins

items.q: A client squeezed an infected pimple on the upper lip and now has a spreading infection. Which complication should the nurse be most concerned about?
o: Spread of infection to the cavernous sinus
Spread of infection to the sigmoid sinus
Spread of infection to the subclavian vein through the external jugular vein
Spread of infection to the parotid gland through the deep facial vein
items.w: The nose and upper lip are the dangerous area of the face. Their blood drains into the anterior facial vein, which connects with the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins and through the deep facial vein and pterygoid plexus. Infection in this area can therefore travel back into the cavernous sinus inside the skull. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.1: The sigmoid sinus continues as the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen; it is not the route from the dangerous area.
x.2: The external jugular vein drains into the subclavian vein, but it does not drain the nose and upper lip.
x.3: The deep facial vein links the anterior facial vein to the pterygoid plexus, not to the parotid gland.

m.1: confuses cavernous and sigmoid sinus

items.q: A client has an infected lesion on the upper lip. Arrange the deep venous route by which the infection can reach the cavernous sinus.
o: Infected area of the nose and upper lip
items.w: Infection in the dangerous area drains into the anterior facial vein. The deep facial vein connects the anterior facial vein to the pterygoid plexus of veins, and the plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus, so organisms can travel this deep route into the skull. A second route runs from the anterior facial vein through the ophthalmic veins. (Anatomy L5 slides)

items.q: A nurse reviews the venous anatomy of the parotid region. The retromandibular vein forms inside the {1} by the union of the maxillary vein and the {2} vein; its posterior branch then joins the {3} vein to form the external jugular vein.
items.w: The retromandibular (posterior facial) vein is formed inside the parotid gland by the maxillary and superficial temporal veins. At the lower pole of the parotid it divides: the posterior branch joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein, and the anterior branch joins the anterior facial vein to form the common facial vein, which drains into the IJV. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.0:1: The retromandibular vein forms inside the parotid gland, not the submandibular gland.
x.0:2: The cavernous sinus is inside the skull and receives the ophthalmic veins.
x.1:1: The supraorbital vein joins the supratrochlear vein to form the anterior facial vein.
x.1:2: The lingual vein is a tributary of the internal jugular vein.
x.2:1: The anterior facial vein joins the ANTERIOR branch to form the common facial vein.
x.2:2: The transverse cervical vein is a tributary of the external jugular vein.

m.1:1: mixes up anterior facial and retromandibular formation
m.2:1: mixes up anterior and posterior divisions

items.q: A nurse notices a distended vein crossing superficial to a client's sternomastoid muscle. Which veins unite to form this vein?
o: The posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein
The maxillary and superficial temporal veins
The anterior facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein
The internal jugular and subclavian veins
items.w: The vein running superficial to sternomastoid is the external jugular vein. It forms from the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein, descends over sternomastoid and ends in the subclavian vein. Its tributaries are the transverse cervical, suprascapular and anterior jugular veins. (Anatomy L5 slides, slide exercise)

x.1: These form the anterior facial vein at the medial angle of the eye.
x.2: These form the retromandibular vein inside the parotid gland.
x.3: These form the common facial vein, which drains into the IJV.
x.4: These form the brachiocephalic vein.

m.1: mixes up formation of the facial veins
m.2: mixes up formation of the facial veins
m.3: mixes up anterior and posterior divisions

items.q: A client has an internal jugular central line. Which veins should the nurse recognize as tributaries of the internal jugular vein? Select all that apply.
items.w: The internal jugular vein begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen and receives the pharyngeal, common facial, lingual, superior thyroid and middle thyroid veins before joining the subclavian vein. The transverse cervical, suprascapular and anterior jugular veins belong to the external jugular vein. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.5: The transverse cervical vein drains into the external jugular vein.
x.6: The suprascapular vein drains into the external jugular vein.
x.7: The anterior jugular vein drains into the external jugular vein.

m.5: mixes up IJV and EJV tributaries
m.6: mixes up IJV and EJV tributaries
m.7: mixes up IJV and EJV tributaries

items.q: A nurse states that the external jugular vein ends by draining into the internal jugular vein.
items.w: False. The external jugular vein descends superficial to sternomastoid and ends in the SUBCLAVIAN vein; the subclavian vein then joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. (Anatomy L5 slides)

x.0: The external jugular vein ends in the subclavian vein, not the internal jugular vein.

items.q: A nurse traces the venous drainage from a client's face to the heart. Arrange the veins in the order blood passes through them.
items.w: The anterior facial vein joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein. The internal jugular joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein, and the right and left brachiocephalic veins unite to form the superior vena cava. (Anatomy L5 slides)

items.q: A nurse explains an ECG to an anxious client before attaching the electrodes. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
o: It records the electrical activity of your heart over time from the skin surface.
It measures how much blood flows through your heart with each beat.
It measures the pressure inside your coronary arteries.
It sends a small current into your heart to test the valves.
items.w: The heart's electrical activity creates potential differences that the body, a good conductor, carries to the skin, where electrodes record them. The ECG is a measure of the electrical activity of the heart per unit time. It does not measure blood flow through the heart, so a normal tracing says nothing directly about how much blood is pumped. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: The ECG explicitly does NOT measure the flow of blood through the heart.
x.2: The ECG records electrical potential differences, not pressures.
x.3: The electrodes only pick up potential differences generated by the heart; the body conducts them to the skin.

m.1: thinks the ECG measures blood flow

items.q: A nurse reviews a client's 12-lead ECG. Which group of leads records the potential difference between two active electrodes?
items.w: The standard 12-lead ECG has six limb leads in the frontal plane and six chest leads in the horizontal plane. Of the limb leads, I, II and III are bipolar (standard) leads that record the difference between two active electrodes; their axes form Einthoven's equilateral triangle. aVR, aVL and aVF are unipolar augmented leads that compare one active electrode with a zero-potential electrode. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: These are the unipolar (augmented) limb leads: an active electrode against an electrode at zero potential.
x.2: These are the precordial (chest) leads, which look at the horizontal plane.
x.3: These are the leads that view the inferior heart; aVF is unipolar.

m.1: mixes up bipolar and augmented leads
m.3: confuses lead views with lead types

items.q: A nurse is reading a client's 12-lead ECG to localize a problem. Match each group of leads to the part of the heart it views best.
items.w: Each lead is like a picture of the heart from one direction. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the left lateral wall; V1 and V2 look at the septum; V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall; and II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall. Knowing these views lets ST changes be matched to the region involved. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.4: None of these lead groups is described as giving a posterior view.

rs.0: A client's ECG shows changes in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which part of the heart should the nurse recognize these leads view?
rs.1: A nurse notes abnormalities only in leads V1 and V2. Which part of the heart do these leads view best?
rs.2: A client's ECG shows changes confined to leads V3 and V4. Which part of the heart should the nurse associate with these leads?
rs.3: A nurse sees ECG changes in leads II, III and aVF. Which part of the heart do these leads view?

items.q: A nurse notes a tall upright QRS complex in one lead of a client's ECG. What does this deflection tell the nurse about the electrical current?
o: The current is flowing toward that lead's recording electrode.
The current is flowing away from that lead's recording electrode.
More blood is being pumped through that part of the heart.
items.w: A deflection's direction depends on the direction of current relative to the recording electrode. Current flowing toward the electrode gives an upward deflection and current flowing away gives a downward deflection. An upright QRS in a lead therefore means ventricular depolarization is heading toward that electrode. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: Current flowing away from the electrode gives a downward deflection.
x.2: Ventricular repolarization is shown by the T wave, not the QRS.
x.3: The ECG does not measure blood flow.

m.1: reverses the deflection rule
m.3: thinks the ECG measures blood flow

items.q: While measuring a client's rhythm strip at standard paper speed, the nurse counts the width of one large box. What time does one large box represent?
items.w: At the standard paper speed of 25 mm/sec, each small 1-mm box horizontally equals 0.04 s, and a large box (5 small boxes) equals 0.20 s. Vertically, one large box equals 0.5 mV. Durations are read horizontally and amplitudes vertically. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: 0.04 s is one small (1 mm) box.
x.2: 0.5 mV is the VERTICAL value of one large box (voltage, not time).
x.3: 25 mm/s is the paper speed, not the value of a box.

m.1: confuses small and large boxes
m.2: mixes up horizontal and vertical scales

items.q: A nurse measures a client's PR interval and counts 5 small boxes at standard paper speed. What is the PR interval in seconds?
items.w: Each small box at 25 mm/sec is 0.04 s. Setup: 5 small boxes x 0.04 s per box = 0.20 s. A PR interval of 0.20 s is at the upper limit of normal (0.12-0.20 s). (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: 0.04 s is the value of a single small box; it was not multiplied by 5.
x.2: 1 s uses the large-box value (0.20 s) for each small box.
x.3: 5 is the number of boxes, not seconds.

near.0.04: 0.04 is one small box; multiply by the 5 boxes counted.
near.1: 1 uses 0.20 s (a large box) for each small box.
near.5: 5 is the box count; multiply by 0.04 s per box.
near.0.5: 0.5 mV is the vertical value of a large box, not time.

items.q: A nurse notes that the ECG paper moves at 25 mm/s, so each 1-mm small box equals 0.04 s.
items.w: True. At 25 mm per second, 1 mm takes 1/25 s = 0.04 s; five small boxes make a large box of 0.20 s. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: This statement is true: 1 mm at 25 mm/s is 0.04 s.

items.q: A nurse teaches a client what each part of the ECG tracing shows. Match each ECG component to the electrical event it represents.

choices: Atrial depolarization plus the delay in the AV junction
Blood flow through the heart valves

items.w: Each ECG component maps to an electrical event in the conduction sequence SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. The P wave is atrial depolarization, the QRS is ventricular depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization. The PR interval covers atrial depolarization plus the delay in the AV junction (AV node and bundle of His). (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.4: The ECG does not measure blood flow through the heart.

m.4: thinks the ECG measures blood flow

rs.0: A nurse points to the P wave on a client's ECG. Which electrical event does it represent?
rs.1: A client asks what the tall spike on the ECG means. Which event does the QRS complex represent?
rs.2: A nurse explains the T wave on a client's tracing. Which electrical event does it represent?
rs.3: A nurse measures a client's PR interval. Which events does this interval include?

items.q: A nursing student asks why there is a pause between the P wave and the QRS complex on a client's ECG. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
o: The delay in the AV junction gives the atria time to contract before the ventricles contract.
The pause lets the ventricles repolarize before the next beat.
The pause is the time the coronary arteries need to fill.
The pause occurs because the SA node fires twice per beat.
items.w: The PR interval includes atrial depolarization plus a deliberate delay in the AV junction (AV node and bundle of His). The delay allows time for the atria to contract and finish filling the ventricles before ventricular depolarization starts. That is why the normal PR interval is 0.12-0.20 s rather than almost zero. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.1: Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, after the QRS.
x.2: Coronary filling is linked to diastole, not to the PR interval.
x.3: The SA node fires once per beat; the pause is conduction delay in the AV node and bundle of His.

m.1: places repolarization in the PR interval

items.q: A nurse reviews measurements from several clients' ECGs. Which values are within normal limits? Select all that apply.
items.w: Normal intervals: PR 0.12-0.20 s, QRS 0.08-0.10 s and QT 0.40-0.43 s. Note: the rhythm-analysis slide gives a wider normal QRS range of 0.04-0.12 s (1-3 boxes), while the intervals slide says 0.08-0.10 s; 0.08 s is normal by both. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.3: A PR above 0.20 s is prolonged, as in first-degree AV block.
x.4: A QRS wider than 0.12 s is wide, as when the impulse starts in a ventricle.
x.5: 0.08 s is below the 0.12 s lower limit of a normal PR interval.

m.3: accepts a prolonged PR as normal
m.4: accepts a wide QRS as normal

items.q: A nurse analyzes a client's rhythm strip. Arrange the steps of rhythm analysis in the correct order.
items.w: Rhythm analysis follows five steps: determine regularity from the R-R distances, calculate the rate, assess the P waves (present, alike, regular, one before each QRS), determine the PR interval and determine the QRS duration. Working in the same order every time keeps any abnormality from being missed. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

items.q: A nurse counts 20 small squares between two consecutive R waves on a client's regular rhythm strip. What is the client's heart rate in beats/min?
items.w: Setup: HR = 1500 / number of small squares between R-R = 1500 / 20 = 75 beats/min. The constant 1500 is the number of small squares per minute at 25 mm/s; 300 is the number of large squares per minute and goes with large-square counts. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: 15 divides 300 (the large-square constant) by small squares.
x.2: 100 would need 15 small (3 large) squares between R waves.
x.3: 150 would need 10 small (2 large) squares.

m.1: uses the wrong constant

near.15: 15 used 300 / 20; 300 goes with LARGE squares. Use 1500 / 20.
near.300: 300 is the rate for only 1 large square between R waves.

items.q: A nurse counts 3 large squares between consecutive R waves on a client's regular rhythm strip. What is the heart rate in beats/min?
items.w: Setup: HR = 300 / number of large squares between R-R = 300 / 3 = 100 beats/min. The quick sequence for large boxes is 300, 150, 100, 75 for 1, 2, 3 and 4 boxes. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.1: 500 divides 1500 (the small-square constant) by large squares.
x.2: 75 is the rate for 4 large squares.
x.3: 150 is the rate for 2 large squares.

m.1: uses the wrong constant

near.500: 500 used 1500 / 3; 1500 goes with SMALL squares. Use 300 / 3.
near.75: 75 is the rate for 4 large squares, not 3.

items.q: A nurse uses the quick count on a client's rhythm strip: the R wave lands on a heavy line and the next R wave is 2 large boxes away. The heart rate is about ____ beats/min.
items.w: Find an R wave on a heavy line and count large boxes to the next R wave: 1 box = 300, 2 boxes = 150, 3 boxes = 100, 4 boxes = 75. This is the same as 300 divided by the number of large boxes. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.1: 300 is the rate when the next R wave is only 1 large box away.
x.2: 100 is the rate for 3 large boxes.
x.3: 75 is the rate for 4 large boxes.

m.1: counts one box too few

items.q: A client's rhythm strip shows: rate 35 bpm, regular, normal P waves, PR 0.12 s, QRS 0.10 s. Which interpretation should the nurse document?
o: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
items.w: When every P wave is normal, each is followed by a QRS, and the PR and QRS durations are normal, the impulse is starting in the SA node and conducting normally. If such a sinus rhythm is slow (35 bpm here), it is sinus bradycardia; if fast (130 bpm in the example), sinus tachycardia. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: Normal sinus rhythm has these features at a normal rate (90-95 bpm in the slide example), not 35 bpm.
x.2: Sinus tachycardia is a fast sinus rhythm (130 bpm in the slide example).
x.3: Third-degree block has P waves with no relation to the QRS and a wide QRS.
x.4: Mobitz II has some P waves not followed by a QRS.

m.2: reverses brady and tachy
m.3: calls any slow rate complete block

items.q: A nurse notices that a healthy young client's heart rate speeds up with each inspiration and slows with expiration; P waves, PR and QRS are normal. How should the nurse interpret this rhythm?
o: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I
items.w: In sinus arrhythmia every beat is still a normal sinus beat, but the rate varies with breathing: it increases during inspiration and decreases during expiration. The P waves, PR interval and QRS stay normal, which separates it from atrial fibrillation and the AV blocks. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: Atrial fibrillation has no normal P waves and an irregularly irregular rate.
x.2: Mobitz I has a PR that lengthens until a QRS is dropped.
x.3: Sinus tachycardia is a steadily fast sinus rhythm, not one that varies with breathing.
x.4: Atrial flutter shows flutter waves instead of P waves.

m.1: calls any irregular rhythm AF

items.q: A nurse reviews the rhythm strip of an 84-year-old client with atrial fibrillation. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Chaotic atrial activity not originating from the sinus node
A PR interval that lengthens until a beat is dropped
P waves with no relation to the QRS complexes
items.w: In atrial fibrillation the atria have no organized depolarization because impulses are not originating from the sinus node. There are therefore no normal P waves, the atrial rate is usually above 350 per minute, and the chaotic activity produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rate. It is common, affecting 2-4% of people and up to 5-10% of those over 80. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.4: This is second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I.
x.5: Flutter waves belong to atrial flutter.
x.6: This is third-degree AV block.

m.4: mixes up AF and Mobitz I
m.5: mixes up atrial fibrillation and flutter

items.q: A client's rhythm strip shows: rate 60 bpm, regular, normal P waves each followed by a QRS, PR interval 0.36 s, QRS 0.08 s. Which interpretation should the nurse document?
o: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
items.w: In first-degree AV block every impulse still reaches the ventricles, but it is held up too long in the AV node or bundle of His, so the PR interval exceeds 0.20 s. Every P wave is followed by a QRS and the rhythm is regular. Dropped beats would point to second-degree block instead. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: Mobitz I has a PR that keeps lengthening until a QRS is dropped; here every P conducts.
x.2: Mobitz II drops beats with a constant PR.
x.3: Third-degree block has P waves unrelated to the QRS.
x.4: A PR of 0.36 s is above the normal 0.12-0.20 s.

m.1: calls any long PR Mobitz I
m.4: accepts a prolonged PR as normal

items.q: A client's rhythm strip shows the PR interval getting longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, and then the cycle repeats. Which rhythm should the nurse identify?
o: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
items.w: In Mobitz type I each successive atrial impulse meets a longer and longer delay in the AV node until one impulse, usually the 3rd or 4th, fails to get through. The strip shows a progressively lengthening PR and then a P wave without a QRS, giving a regularly irregular rhythm. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: Mobitz II drops beats suddenly with no PR prolongation.
x.2: First-degree block has a long but constant PR and no dropped beats.
x.3: Third-degree block has no relation at all between P waves and QRS complexes.
x.4: Atrial fibrillation has no normal P waves.

m.1: mixes up Mobitz I and II

items.q: A client's rhythm strip shows a constant PR interval of 0.14 s, but occasionally a P wave is not followed by a QRS. The nurse recognizes the block is typically located where?
o: In the AV node, with progressive delay
items.w: This is second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II: conduction is all or nothing, so there is no PR prolongation, but some P waves are completely blocked. The block typically lies in the bundle of His, below the AV node, unlike Mobitz I where the delay builds up in the AV node itself. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: The SA node generates the P waves, which are present and normal here.
x.2: Purkinje fibers are not given as the usual site of Mobitz II block.
x.3: Progressive AV-nodal delay describes Mobitz type I.

m.3: mixes up Mobitz I and II

items.q: A client in third-degree AV block has a ventricular rate of 40 bpm and a QRS wider than 0.12 s. Which explanation of the wide QRS is accurate?
o: The impulse originates in a ventricle, so conduction through the ventricles is inefficient.
The AV node is conducting slowly, which lengthens the QRS.
Flutter waves are merging with the QRS.
Sympathetic stimulation is speeding conduction through the bundle of His.
items.w: In third-degree block nothing passes through the AV junction, so the atria and ventricles form impulses independently. Without atrial impulses the ventricles' own pacemaker takes over at about 30-45 beats/minute. Because that impulse starts in a ventricle instead of travelling down the normal conduction system, ventricular conduction is inefficient and the QRS is wide and bizarre. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide note (REMEMBER))

x.1: Slow AV-nodal conduction lengthens the PR interval, not the QRS.
x.2: Flutter waves belong to atrial flutter, not complete block.
x.3: Sympathetic stimulation hastens conduction; it would not widen the QRS.

m.1: confuses PR and QRS prolongation

items.q: A nurse reviews the AV blocks before a cardiology rotation. Match each block to its defining feature.

choices: PR interval longer than 0.20 s with every P conducted
PR lengthens progressively until a P wave is not conducted
Constant PR with occasional P waves completely blocked
Atria and ventricles beat independently of each other
No P waves and an irregularly irregular rate

items.w: The AV blocks are graded by how many impulses get through. First degree: all get through but slowly (PR > 0.20 s). Mobitz I: delay builds until one fails. Mobitz II: all-or-nothing conduction, usually in the bundle of His. Third degree: complete block, so atria and ventricles are independent and a ventricular pacemaker drives the ventricles at 30-45 beats/minute. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.4: This describes atrial fibrillation, not an AV block.

m.4: mixes up AF and AV block

rs.0: A client is diagnosed with first-degree AV block. Which ECG feature should the nurse expect?
rs.1: A client has second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I. Which ECG feature defines it?
rs.2: A client has second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II. Which ECG feature defines it?
rs.3: A client is in third-degree AV block. Which statement describes the relationship between the atria and ventricles?

items.q: A nurse states that in second-degree AV block Mobitz type II, the PR interval lengthens progressively before a beat is dropped.
items.w: False. In Mobitz type II conduction is all or nothing: the PR interval stays constant (0.14 s in the slide example) and occasional P waves are suddenly blocked. Progressive PR lengthening is Mobitz type I. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.0: Progressive PR lengthening is Mobitz type I; Mobitz II has a constant PR.

m.0: mixes up Mobitz I and II

items.q: A client's ECG shows a positive QRS in lead I and a negative QRS in aVF. How should the nurse interpret the QRS axis?
items.w: The quadrant method uses lead I and aVF. Positive in both means a normal axis; positive in I but negative in aVF means the vector points up and to the left, left axis deviation; negative in I but positive in aVF is right axis deviation; negative in both is right superior (indeterminate) deviation. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), slide exercise)

x.1: A normal axis has a positive QRS in both lead I and aVF.
x.2: Right axis deviation is negative in lead I and positive in aVF.
x.3: This is negative in both lead I and aVF.

m.1: ignores the negative aVF
m.2: reverses left and right axis rules

items.q: A nurse examines a client's 12-lead ECG and finds the QRS negative in lead I and negative in lead II. Which axis should the nurse report?
items.w: When the QRS is negative in lead I the vector points to the right, and when it is also negative in the inferior leads the vector points upward. Up and to the right is the region between +180 and -90 degrees, called right superior axis deviation or indeterminate (extended right) axis. Note: the slide asks this with lead II; its quick table uses lead I and aVF, where negative-negative gives the same answer. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II), in-class question)

x.1: A normal axis is positive in lead I.
x.2: Left axis deviation keeps lead I positive.
x.3: Plain right axis deviation still has a positive aVF/inferior lead.

m.1: ignores negative lead I
m.3: misses the superior component

items.q: A nurse calculates a client's mean QRS axis. A normal axis lies between {1} and {2}; an axis between +110 and +180 degrees is called {3}.
items.w: The QRS axis is read on a circle in the frontal plane where 0 degrees points to the client's left and the scale rotates clockwise, so +90 points down. The normal axis lies between -30 and +110 degrees; -30 to -90 is left axis deviation; +110 to +180 is right axis deviation; +180 to -90 is indeterminate (extended right). (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.0:1: -90 degrees is the far end of left axis deviation.
x.0:2: 0 degrees is lead I's direction, inside the normal range, not its limit.
x.1:1: +180 degrees is the far end of right axis deviation.
x.1:2: +90 degrees (aVF) is inside the normal range, not its limit.
x.2:1: Left axis deviation is -30 to -90 degrees.

m.0:1: places the normal limit too far left
m.1:1: places the normal limit too far right
m.2:1: reverses left and right axis rules

items.q: A nurse explains that the normal QRS axis points leftward and downward because most of the ventricular mass is in the left ventricle.
items.w: True. When the ventricles depolarize in a normal heart, the current flows leftward and downward because most of the ventricular mass is in the left ventricle. (Physiology L7 slides (ECG II))

x.1: This statement is true: the left ventricle's mass pulls the axis leftward and down.

items.q: A nurse reads a client's QRS axis as +150 degrees and documents it as a normal axis.
items.w: False. The normal axis is -30 to +110 degrees. +150 degrees falls between +110 and +180, which is right axis deviation. (Physiology L6 slides (ECG I))

x.0: +150 degrees is right axis deviation, not normal.

m.0: accepts right axis deviation as normal

items.q: A client's heart rate is 80 beats/min and stroke volume is 75 mL. What is the client's cardiac output in L/min?
items.w: Setup: cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 80 beats/min x 75 mL/beat = 6000 mL/min = 6 L/min. The slide's resting example is 70 x 70 = 4900 mL/min, about 5 L/min. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: 155 added heart rate and stroke volume instead of multiplying them.
x.2: 6000 is the answer in mL/min; it was not converted to L/min.
x.3: 1.07 divided stroke volume by heart rate.

near.155: 155 added HR and SV; cardiac output is HR x SV.
near.6000: 6000 is mL/min; divide by 1000 for L/min.
near.1.07: 1.07 divided SV by HR; multiply them instead.

items.q: A client's echocardiogram shows an end-diastolic volume of 125 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What is the ejection fraction in percent?
items.w: Setup: SV = EDV - ESV = 125 - 50 = 75 mL. EF = SV / EDV x 100 = 75 / 125 x 100 = 60%. The slide's example is 75/120 x 100 = 62.5%, and the normal range is 50-75%. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: 40 divided ESV by EDV (50/125) instead of SV by EDV.
x.2: 75 is the stroke volume in mL, not the ejection fraction.
x.3: 0.6 forgot to multiply by 100.

m.1: uses ESV instead of SV

near.40: 40 is ESV/EDV x 100; use SV (EDV - ESV) on top.
near.75: 75 is the stroke volume in mL; divide it by EDV.
near.150: 150 is EDV/SV x 100; the fraction is upside down.

items.q: A client recovering from a myocardial infarction has an ejection fraction of 30%. How should the nurse interpret this value?
o: It is consistent with a failing heart.
It is within the normal resting range.
It is the expected value during strenuous exercise.
It means the client's preload is increased.
items.w: Ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic volume ejected with each stroke and is a good index of ventricular function. A healthy heart ejects 50-75% at rest and up to 90% in strenuous exercise; a failing heart may eject 30% or less. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: The normal resting ejection fraction is 50-75%.
x.2: During strenuous exercise EF can rise to as much as 90%, not fall to 30%.
x.3: EF is the fraction of EDV ejected; a low EF reflects poor ventricular function, not raised preload.

m.1: thinks 30% EF is normal

items.q: A nurse explains why a large client's cardiac output is reported as cardiac index. Which definition should the nurse give?
o: Cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area
The difference between resting cardiac output and the maximum output
The volume pumped by each ventricle per beat
The percentage of end-diastolic volume ejected with each beat
items.w: Cardiac output depends on body size, so it is normalized as the cardiac index: cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area, normally 3.2 L/min/m2. Cardiac reserve is a different idea: how much output can rise from rest to maximum. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: That is cardiac reserve.
x.2: That is stroke volume.
x.3: That is ejection fraction.

m.1: confuses cardiac index and cardiac reserve

items.q: A client receives a drug that stimulates the vagus nerve. Match each part of the heart to the parasympathetic effect the nurse should expect.
items.w: The vagus nerve supplies mainly the atria, including the SA and AV nodes, and its supply to the ventricles is sparse. It therefore slows the SA node's rate of depolarization (lower heart rate), increases AV nodal delay and reduces atrial contractility, but has no effect on ventricular muscle. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.4: Increased contractility is a sympathetic effect.

m.4: gives parasympathetic a sympathetic effect

rs.0: A client receives a vagal stimulant. What effect should the nurse expect at the SA node?
rs.1: A client has strong vagal stimulation. What effect should the nurse expect at the AV node?
rs.2: A nurse anticipates the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on atrial muscle. What is it?
rs.3: A client has increased parasympathetic activity. What effect should the nurse expect on ventricular muscle?

items.q: A client is frightened and has a surge of sympathetic activity. Which cardiac effects should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Epinephrine secretion from the adrenal medulla
items.w: Sympathetic nerves supply the SA node, AV node and ventricles. They speed depolarization to threshold (higher heart rate), increase AV excitability and decrease AV delay, hasten conduction through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, increase atrial and ventricular contractility, and stimulate the adrenal medulla to release epinephrine, which adds to these effects. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.4: Increased AV nodal delay is a parasympathetic effect.
x.5: Decreased atrial contractility is a parasympathetic effect.
x.6: No effect on ventricular muscle is the parasympathetic pattern; sympathetic stimulation increases it.

m.4: mixes up sympathetic and parasympathetic AV effects

items.q: A nurse explains that under resting conditions parasympathetic discharge dominates control of heart rate.
items.w: True. Heart rate is set by the balance between vagal inhibition of the SA node and sympathetic stimulation, and at rest parasympathetic discharge dominates. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: This statement is true: at rest the vagus dominates.

items.q: A client receives a fluid bolus that increases end-diastolic volume, and the stroke volume rises. Which mechanism explains the stronger contraction?
o: Greater stretch brings cardiac fibers closer to their optimum length, so contraction force increases.
Sympathetic stimulation shifts the Frank-Starling curve to the left.
Afterload increases, forcing the ventricle to contract harder.
items.w: This is the Frank-Starling law, the intrinsic control of stroke volume. Resting cardiac fiber length is shorter than the optimum length for maximum tension. Extra filling raises EDV, stretches the fibers closer to optimum and so increases the force of the next contraction, raising stroke volume. The extent of filling is the preload. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: That is extrinsic control, which raises contractility at any EDV; the bolus works through intrinsic control.
x.2: Afterload is arterial pressure; a fluid bolus acts on preload (EDV).
x.3: Parasympathetic stimulation has no effect on ventricular muscle.

m.1: confuses intrinsic and extrinsic control
m.2: mixes up preload and afterload

items.q: A nurse defines afterload as the end-diastolic volume that stretches the ventricle before it contracts.
items.w: False. That definition is preload (the load before contraction, the end-diastolic volume). Afterload is the load against which the ventricle pumps, i.e. the pressure in the artery (arterial blood pressure). (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.0: End-diastolic volume is preload; afterload is arterial pressure.

items.q: A nurse encourages a client on bed rest to do leg exercises and deep breathing. Which factors increase venous return to the heart? Select all that apply.
o: Skeletal muscle contraction compressing the veins
The fall in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration
One-way valves in the large veins
Veins storing a larger share of the blood volume
items.w: Venous return rises when less blood sits in the capacitance veins. The skeletal muscle pump squeezes veins, the respiratory pump lowers intrathoracic pressure to about -5 mmHg in inspiration, sympathetic vasoconstriction raises venous pressure, the cardiac suction effect pulls the AV valves down during ventricular contraction, and venous valves every 2-4 cm stop backflow on standing. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.4: When veins store MORE blood, less returns to the heart.
x.5: Parasympathetic stimulation has no effect on veins.

m.4: reverses the capacitance effect

items.q: A client's oxygen uptake is 250 mL/min, arterial O2 content is 200 mL/L and pulmonary artery (mixed venous) O2 content is 150 mL/L. Using the Fick principle, what is the cardiac output in L/min?
items.w: Setup: cardiac output = O2 uptake / (arterial O2 - venous O2) = 250 mL/min / (200 - 150) mL/L = 250 / 50 = 5 L/min. Venous blood is sampled from the pulmonary artery. The slide example is 200 / (200 - 160) = 5 L/min. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: 1.25 divided O2 uptake by the ARTERIAL content (250/200) instead of the A-V difference.
x.2: 0.2 divided the A-V difference by O2 uptake; the fraction is upside down.
x.3: 12500 multiplied O2 uptake by the A-V difference.

m.1: divides by arterial instead of A-V difference

near.1.25: 1.25 divided by arterial O2; divide by the A-V difference (200 - 150).
near.1.67: 1.67 divided by venous O2 (250/150); use the A-V difference.
near.0.2: 0.2 is upside down; O2 uptake goes on top.
near.12500: 12500 multiplied; divide O2 uptake by the A-V difference.

items.q: A nurse reviews several clients' conditions. Which conditions increase cardiac output? Select all that apply.
items.w: Among pathological states, hyperthyroidism, anemia and fever increase cardiac output. Hypothyroidism, myocardial damage and failure, valvular heart disease, arrhythmias, and hemorrhage and shock decrease it. Exercise, emotion, posture and pregnancy alter it physiologically. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.3: Hypothyroidism decreases cardiac output.
x.4: Hemorrhage and shock decrease cardiac output.
x.5: Valvular heart disease decreases cardiac output.

m.3: reverses thyroid effects

items.q: A nurse is teaching a community group about heart failure. Which cause should the nurse identify as the most common?
items.w: Heart failure is the inability of the heart to provide a cardiac output that keeps pace with the body's demand; it may be left, right or biventricular. The most common cause is a heart attack (myocardial infarction), followed by working against increased afterload, as in hypertension or aortic valve stenosis. (Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output))

x.1: Hypertension causes failure by raising afterload; it is listed second, after myocardial infarction.
x.2: Anemia increases cardiac output; it is not listed as a common cause of failure.
x.3: Hyperthyroidism increases cardiac output; it is not listed as a common cause of failure.

m.1: puts afterload causes first

items.q: A client with coronary artery disease begins an exercise program. How does the heart meet its extra oxygen demand during exercise?
o: By increasing coronary blood flow, because extraction is already 60-70% at rest
By raising oxygen extraction from 25% to 70%
By parasympathetic vasodilation of the coronary arteries
items.w: Cardiac muscle is packed with mitochondria (up to 40% of the cell) and works by aerobic metabolism, so at rest it already extracts 60-70% of the oxygen delivered, compared with about 25% in other tissues. Because little extra can be extracted, more oxygen can reach the heart only by increasing coronary blood flow. This is why narrowed coronaries cause symptoms on effort. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation), slide exercise)

x.1: 25% is the extraction of other tissues; the heart already extracts 60-70% at rest.
x.2: The heart turns to anaerobic glycolysis only in ischemia, producing lactic acid.
x.3: Parasympathetic influences on coronary vessels are minor and only weakly vasodilatory.

m.1: thinks the heart can raise extraction a lot

items.q: A nurse states that resting coronary blood flow is about 225-250 mL/min, about 5% of cardiac output.
items.w: True. Coronary blood flow in humans at rest is about 225-250 ml/minute, about 5% of the cardiac output. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.1: This statement is true: about 225-250 mL/min, 5% of cardiac output.

items.q: A client with stable angina asks why the chest pain happens. Which metabolic change during ischemia contributes to cardiac pain?
o: Increased oxidation of free fatty acids
Storage of extra glucose in cardiac muscle
items.w: The heart normally uses mainly free fatty acids, and to a lesser extent glucose and lactate, by aerobic metabolism. In ischemic (anaerobic) conditions it derives energy from anaerobic glycolysis, which forms lactic acid, one of the causes of cardiac pain. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.1: Free fatty acids are the heart's main fuel under normal aerobic conditions.
x.2: Ischemia means oxygen supply is short, so aerobic mitochondrial metabolism falls.
x.3: Storing glucose is not a change the heart makes in ischemia.

m.1: thinks FFA use causes pain

items.q: A nurse explains to a student why the left ventricle receives most of its coronary blood flow during diastole. Which explanation is accurate?
o: The contracting left ventricle compresses its coronary vessels, and the open aortic valve partly blocks their entrance.
Aortic pressure is lowest during systole.
The pressure gradient from aorta to left ventricle is larger in systole than in diastole.
The right ventricle compresses the left coronary vessels during systole.
items.w: During systole the powerful left ventricle squeezes the coronary arteries running through its wall, and the open aortic valve partially blocks the coronary openings. The LV pressure (121 mmHg) even slightly exceeds aortic pressure (120), so the gradient is about -1 mmHg. In diastole the LV pressure is 0 and the gradient is 80 mmHg, so most LV flow occurs then. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.1: Aortic pressure is highest in systole (120 mmHg on the slide).
x.2: In systole the LV pressure (121) slightly exceeds the aorta (120), so the gradient is -1 mmHg; in diastole it is 80.
x.3: The compression comes from the powerful left ventricle's own muscle.

m.1: reverses aortic pressure timing
m.2: reverses the LV pressure gradient

items.q: A nurse reviews why myocardial infarction most often begins in one part of the heart. Which region is most prone to ischemic damage?
o: The subendocardial layer of the left ventricle
All layers of the heart equally
items.w: During systole blood flow to the subendocardial surface of the left ventricle almost stops, because the contracting LV wall compresses the vessels most at its inner layer. This region therefore depends on diastole for its supply, is prone to ischemic damage and is the most common site of myocardial infarction. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.1: Right ventricular flow is not much affected in systole because the aorta-RV gradient stays high (95 mmHg).
x.2: The pressure gradient from the aorta to the right atrium is larger in systole, so flow there is preserved.
x.3: Flow is not equal; the LV subendocardium loses almost all flow in systole.

m.1: thinks the RV is most at risk

items.q: A client with a heart rate of 150 beats/min complains of chest tightness. Which explanation should the nurse give for reduced coronary blood flow in tachycardia?
o: Diastole becomes shorter, so there is less time for coronary flow.
Systole becomes shorter, so the vessels are compressed less and flow rises.
Aortic diastolic pressure rises with heart rate.
Parasympathetic activity constricts the coronary arteries.
items.w: Most left ventricular coronary flow occurs in diastole. When the heart rate increases, the diastolic period is shortened, so coronary blood flow to the heart is reduced, which can produce ischemic chest tightness. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.1: Tachycardia shortens diastole, and that is when most LV flow occurs.
x.2: A LOW aortic diastolic pressure reduces coronary flow; rate does not raise it as an explanation here.
x.3: Parasympathetic influences on coronary vessels are minor and weakly vasodilatory.

m.1: thinks tachycardia improves coronary flow

items.q: A nurse reviews conditions that reduce blood flow to the left ventricle. Which conditions decrease left ventricular coronary flow? Select all that apply.
items.w: In aortic stenosis the left ventricular pressure is very high in systole and compresses the coronary arteries more. A low aortic diastolic pressure lowers the driving pressure for coronary flow. Tachycardia shortens diastole, when most LV flow occurs. Metabolites such as adenosine, CO2 and H+ do the opposite and dilate coronary vessels. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.3: Adenosine is a coronary vasodilator that increases flow.
x.4: Increased CO2 and H+ cause coronary vasodilation and increase flow.

m.3: thinks metabolites constrict coronaries
m.4: thinks metabolites constrict coronaries

items.q: A nurse caring for a client with myocardial ischemia reviews local factors that dilate the coronary arteries. Which factors cause coronary vasodilation? Select all that apply.
items.w: Coronary blood flow shows considerable autoregulation driven by local metabolism. Lack of oxygen and increased local CO2, H+, K+, lactate, prostaglandins, adenosine and adenine nucleotides all dilate coronary vessels. Adenosine, formed from ATP during cardiac metabolic activity, is singled out as a coronary vasodilator. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation), slide note (NOTE))

x.5: It is the LACK of oxygen that dilates coronary vessels.
x.6: Alpha-adrenergic stimulation causes coronary vasoconstriction.

m.5: reverses the hypoxia effect

items.q: A client's sympathetic activity rises during exercise and the coronary arteries dilate. Which mechanism explains this dilation in the intact body?
o: Beta-1 stimulation raises heart rate and contractility, releasing vasodilator metabolites.
Direct stimulation of coronary alpha receptors
items.w: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine, which acts on beta-1 receptors to increase heart rate and force of contraction. The extra work releases vasodilator metabolites, so coronary vessels dilate. This indirect effect wins in the intact body. The direct effect on coronary arteries is vasoconstriction, seen when beta blockers remove the inotropic and chronotropic effects. In shock, this preserves heart flow while other organs are compromised. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation), slide exercise)

x.1: The direct effect of noradrenergic stimulation on coronary arteries is vasoconstriction.
x.2: Parasympathetic influences are minor and only weakly vasodilatory.
x.3: Metabolism rises with sympathetic stimulation; that rise produces the vasodilator metabolites.

m.1: thinks the direct sympathetic effect dilates

items.q: A nurse states that the direct effect of noradrenergic stimulation on the coronary arteries is vasodilation.
items.w: False. The DIRECT effect is vasoconstriction (alpha receptors), seen when beta-adrenergic blockers remove the increase in heart rate and contractility. The vasodilation seen in the intact body is indirect, through vasodilator metabolites. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.0: The direct noradrenergic effect is vasoconstriction; dilation is indirect.

m.0: thinks the direct sympathetic effect dilates

items.q: A client describes chest discomfort to the nurse. Which features are typical of angina pectoris? Select all that apply.
o: Tightness or pain in the middle of the chest lasting a few minutes
Pain radiating to the inner side of the left arm
ST-segment elevation in the respective leads
At least 75% of the coronary lumen blocked by thrombus
items.w: In ischemic heart disease (angina pectoris) coronary flow is reduced by atherosclerotic plaque. The client feels retrosternal tightness or pain for a few minutes, often radiating to the inner side of the left arm; it is brought on by effort and relieved by rest. MI is different: a thrombus blocks at least 75% of the lumen. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation))

x.4: ST elevation is the ECG change of myocardial infarction.
x.5: This describes myocardial infarction.

m.4: mixes up angina and MI ECG changes
m.5: mixes up angina and MI

items.q: A client with chest pain has a 12-lead ECG. Which finding should the nurse report as consistent with myocardial infarction rather than angina?
o: ST-segment elevation in the leads facing the affected area
ST-segment depression in the leads facing the affected area
items.w: The ECG distinguishes the two: in ischemic heart disease the ST segment is depressed in the respective leads, as on a treadmill test with horizontal ST depression; in myocardial infarction the ST segment is elevated in the respective leads. Cardiac enzymes, echocardiography, stress tests and angiography complete the work-up. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation), slide note (NOTE))

x.1: ST depression is the ECG change of ischemic heart disease (angina), as on an exercise test.
x.2: A PR above 0.20 s is first-degree AV block.
x.3: A wide QRS indicates an impulse starting in a ventricle.

m.1: mixes up angina and MI ECG changes

items.q: A nurse screens a client for ischemic heart disease. Which findings are risk factors? Select all that apply.
items.w: The listed risk factors for ischemic heart disease are cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, increased lipids (cholesterol) and other factors such as lack of exercise and anxiety. HDL is the exception among lipids: high HDL lowers coronary risk. (Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation); HDL point from Biochemistry L5 slides)

x.5: High HDL-cholesterol is associated with a DECREASED risk of coronary heart disease.
x.6: Anemia is listed as a cause of increased cardiac output, not as an IHD risk factor.

m.5: thinks all cholesterol raises risk

items.q: A client with a deep vein thrombosis of the left leg has a swollen limb that is dusky reddish-blue. How should the nurse interpret this color change?
o: Congestion from impaired venous outflow with deoxygenated blood
items.w: Congestion is a passive process caused by impaired venous outflow, such as a DVT. Red cells stagnate and deoxygenated venous blood accumulates, so the tissue turns dusky reddish-blue (cyanosis). Hyperemia is the opposite: an active arteriolar dilation that fills tissue with oxygenated blood and makes it red. Sudden complete venous obstruction also causes rapid edema and hemorrhage. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: Hyperemia makes tissue red (erythema) from oxygenated blood, not reddish-blue.
x.2: Ischemia is deficient ARTERIAL supply; DVT obstructs venous outflow.
x.3: Infarction is ischemic necrosis; the color described is the stasis of congestion.

m.1: mixes up hyperemia and congestion
m.2: mixes up arterial and venous obstruction

items.q: A nurse is teaching about increased local blood volume. Which situations are examples of hyperemia? Select all that apply.
o: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg
Pulmonary veins in left ventricular failure
items.w: Hyperemia is active: arterioles dilate and more blood flows in, as in acute inflammation, exercising skeletal muscle, the gut after a meal and blushing. Congestion is passive: venous outflow is impaired, as with DVT, a twisted ovarian pedicle or left ventricular failure backing up into the pulmonary veins. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.4: DVT causes acute localized congestion.
x.5: A twisted pedicle obstructs venous outflow: acute localized congestion.
x.6: This is chronic localized (pulmonary) congestion.

m.4: mixes up hyperemia and congestion
m.5: mixes up hyperemia and congestion

items.q: A client with chronic left ventricular failure has sputum containing macrophages filled with hemosiderin. What are these cells called?
items.w: In chronic pulmonary congestion, from chronic left ventricular failure or mitral stenosis, the alveolar capillaries are engorged. Fluid leaks into the alveoli (pulmonary edema) and capillaries rupture so red cells enter the alveoli. Alveolar macrophages phagocytose and degrade the red cells, becoming hemosiderin-laden heart failure cells. Long-standing congestion adds interstitial fibrosis: brown induration of the lung. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells are cardiac histiocytes inside Aschoff bodies of rheumatic fever.
x.2: Foam cells are lipid-filled macrophages and smooth muscle cells in atherosclerotic lesions.
x.3: Aschoff bodies are the pathognomonic lesions of acute rheumatic fever.

m.1: mixes up heart failure cells and Anitschkow cells
m.2: mixes up heart failure cells and foam cells

items.q: A client has long-standing mitral stenosis. Arrange the changes of chronic pulmonary congestion in the order they develop.
o: Transudation of fluid and passage of red cells into the alveoli
Phagocytosis and degradation of the red cells by macrophages
Fibrosis of the interstitium and alveolar septa (brown induration)
items.w: Chronic left ventricular failure or mitral stenosis backs blood up into the alveolar capillaries. Fluid transudes into the alveoli and ruptured capillaries let red cells through; macrophages engulf and degrade the red cells and become hemosiderin-laden heart failure cells. With long-standing congestion, the interstitium and alveolar septa become fibrotic, giving brown induration of the lung. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

items.q: A client with chronic right-sided heart failure has dyspnea, generalized edema and congestion of several organs. Which type of congestion is this?
items.w: Chronic generalized venous congestion is gradual congestion of the whole venous system, caused by chronic right-sided heart failure. Its effects are dyspnea (from pulmonary congestion), chronic venous congestion in different organs and generalized cardiac edema. Acute heart failure instead gives rapid congestion in all viscera. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: Acute generalized congestion follows ACUTE heart failure.
x.2: Localized congestion affects one region, from compression of a vein or left failure in the lung.
x.3: Acute localized congestion follows a sudden complete venous obstruction such as a DVT.

m.1: mixes up acute and chronic generalized congestion

items.q: A nurse cares for several clients with edema. Match each cause to the mechanism that produces the edema.
items.w: Edema has four mechanisms. Venous congestion or sodium and water retention raise capillary hydrostatic pressure; hypoproteinemia lowers plasma colloid osmotic pressure; toxins, hypoxia and chemicals such as histamine increase capillary permeability; and lymphangitis, filariasis, tumors, irradiation fibrosis or lymph node removal obstruct lymphatics. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.4: A rise in colloid osmotic pressure would hold fluid in vessels; edema follows a DECREASE.

m.4: reverses the oncotic effect

rs.0: A malnourished client with hypoproteinemia develops edema. Which mechanism should the nurse identify?
rs.1: A client's inflamed ankle swells as histamine is released. Which mechanism causes this edema?
rs.2: A client with venous congestion develops leg edema. Which mechanism causes it?
rs.3: A client with filariasis develops massive leg swelling. Which mechanism causes the edema?

items.q: A malnourished client's labs are reviewed for nutritional edema. Edema from hypoproteinemia occurs when serum albumin falls below ____.
items.w: Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure causes edema when the plasma proteins that hold fluid in the vessels fall too low. Hypoproteinemia is defined as total plasma proteins below 2.5 gm% or serum albumin below 1.5 gm%; the resulting generalized edema is called nutritional edema. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: 2.5 gm% is the threshold for TOTAL plasma proteins, not albumin.
x.2: 3.5 gm% is not the threshold given; the albumin threshold is 1.5 gm%.

m.1: mixes up albumin and total protein thresholds
