items.q: A nurse assesses several clients for pitting. Which clients would the nurse expect to have non-pitting edema? Select all that apply.
o: A client with a cellulitis-related inflammatory edema
A client with lymphatic edema after lymph node removal
A client with cardiac edema from heart failure
A client with nutritional edema from hypoproteinemia
A client with obstructive venous edema
items.w: Edema is classified by consistency. Pitting edema is seen in generalized edema (cardiac, renal and nutritional) and in obstructive venous edema. Non-pitting edema is seen in inflammatory edema and lymphatic edema. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.2: Cardiac edema is generalized, and generalized edema is pitting.
x.3: Nutritional edema is generalized and pitting.
x.4: Obstructive venous edema is pitting.

m.2: thinks generalized edema is non-pitting
m.4: thinks venous edema is non-pitting

items.q: A nurse states that lymphatic edema, such as that caused by filariasis, is typically pitting.
items.w: False. Lymphatic edema (and inflammatory edema) is NON-pitting. Pitting edema is seen in generalized edema and obstructive venous edema. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.0: Lymphatic edema is non-pitting.

items.q: A nurse explains that sudden occlusion of an artery in an organ with good collateral circulation may produce no effect.
items.w: True. In acute ischemia, organs with good collateral circulation show no effect, while organs with poor collateral circulation undergo infarction. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: This statement is true: good collaterals can prevent damage.

items.q: A client develops a pulmonary infarct after a pulmonary embolism. Which appearance should the nurse expect the infarct to have?
o: No infarct, because arterial occlusion never causes infarction in the lung
items.w: Infarcts are red when blood can seep into the necrotic area: with venous occlusion, in loose tissues like the lung, in tissues with a dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine) and after reperfusion. White infarcts occur where arterial occlusion hits a dense solid organ with end-arterial circulation, which limits seepage of blood. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: White infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial circulation such as heart, spleen and kidney.
x.2: A septic infarct is classified by infection, not color; nothing here suggests infection.
x.3: Pulmonary infarction does occur, e.g. medium emboli in a congested lung.

m.1: thinks lung infarcts are white

items.q: A nurse reviews infarct types. Which situations typically produce a red (hemorrhagic) infarct? Select all that apply.
o: Reperfusion after angioplasty of an occluded artery
Coronary arterial occlusion in the heart
items.w: Red infarcts form where blood can enter the dead tissue: venous occlusion (ovary, testis), loose tissue (lung), dual blood supply (lung, liver, small intestine) and restored flow to a previously occluded site after angioplasty. Heart, spleen and kidney are dense end-arterial organs that give white infarcts. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.4: The kidney is a solid organ with end-arterial circulation: white infarct.
x.5: The spleen gives a white (anemic) infarct.
x.6: The heart gives a white (anemic) infarct.

m.4: thinks solid-organ infarcts are red
m.5: thinks solid-organ infarcts are red

items.q: A client has an infarct of the testis. Which cause should the nurse recognize as most likely for an infarct in this organ?
o: Venous thrombosis, because the testis has a single venous outflow
Arterial occlusion in an organ with a dual blood supply
Chronic ischemia from gradual atherosclerosis with good collaterals
Septic embolism from a lung abscess
items.w: Almost all infarcts (99%) come from thrombosis or embolism, usually arterial. Venous thrombosis causes infarcts mainly in organs with a single venous outflow, such as the testis and ovary, because there is no alternative drainage route once that vein is blocked. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.1: Dual circulation describes the lung, liver and small intestine, not the testis.
x.2: Good collaterals prevent damage; this would not produce an infarct.
x.3: Nothing suggests infection; infection defines a septic infarct, not the usual testicular infarct.

items.q: A nurse states that white (anemic) infarcts typically occur in the lung because of its dual circulation.
items.w: False. The lung, with its loose tissue and dual circulation, gives RED (hemorrhagic) infarcts. White infarcts occur with arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation: heart, spleen and kidney. (Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I))

x.0: The lung gives red infarcts; white infarcts are heart, spleen and kidney.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a postoperative client for thrombosis risk. Which factors make up Virchow's triad? Select all that apply.
o: Stasis or turbulence of blood flow
items.w: Thrombosis is inappropriate activation of normal hemostasis, which is regulated by the vessel wall, platelets and coagulation factors. Virchow's triad names the three primary causes: endothelial injury or dysfunction, alterations in normal blood flow (stasis or turbulence) and hypercoagulability of the blood. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.3: Increased capillary permeability is a mechanism of edema.
x.4: Lymphatic obstruction is a mechanism of edema.
x.5: Arteriolar dilation is hyperemia.

m.3: mixes up edema and thrombosis mechanisms
m.4: mixes up edema and thrombosis mechanisms

items.q: A nurse reviews a client's history for ACQUIRED causes of hypercoagulability. Which findings apply? Select all that apply.
items.w: Hypercoagulability means more coagulation proteins or fewer natural anticoagulants. Hereditary causes include mutations of the factor V and prothrombin genes and antithrombin III deficiency. Acquired causes include prolonged bed rest or immobilization, tissue damage (surgery, burns), hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), disseminated cancer, smoking and DIC. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.5: A factor V gene mutation is a HEREDITARY cause.
x.6: Inherited antithrombin III deficiency is a HEREDITARY cause.

m.5: mixes up hereditary and acquired hypercoagulability
m.6: mixes up hereditary and acquired hypercoagulability

items.q: A client with long-standing hypertension has endothelial dysfunction. Which change in the endothelium favors thrombosis?
o: Decreased production of thrombomodulin and nitric oxide
Decreased production of von Willebrand factor
items.w: Hemodynamic stress such as hypertension, trauma, inflammation, atherosclerosis or hyperlipidemia makes the endothelium dysfunctional. A dysfunctional endothelium produces more procoagulants (thromboplastin, vWF, PAI) and fewer anticoagulants (thrombomodulin, antithrombin III, NO, PA). If the endothelium is lost, exposed matrix lets vWF bind platelets and activates the coagulation cascade. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Antithrombin III is an anticoagulant; dysfunction DECREASES it.
x.2: vWF is a procoagulant; dysfunction INCREASES it.
x.3: Plasminogen activator (PA) is anticoagulant; dysfunction DECREASES it.

m.1: reverses the endothelial effect
m.2: reverses the endothelial effect
m.3: reverses the endothelial effect

items.q: A client with varicose veins asks why sluggish blood flow causes clots. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
o: Slow flow reduces the inflow of fresh blood carrying natural anticoagulants and delays removal of platelet clumps.
Slow flow mechanically tears the endothelium.
Slow flow increases plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
Slow flow lowers the concentration of coagulation proteins.
items.w: Stasis, mainly in veins with obstruction such as varicose veins, reduces the inflow of fresh blood that carries natural anticoagulants and retards the removal of small platelet aggregates. Turbulence (aneurysms, mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation) instead injures endothelial cells. Both stasis and turbulence activate procoagulant secretion and bring platelets and leukocytes into contact with the endothelium. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Mechanical injury to endothelium is the effect of TURBULENCE, not stasis.
x.2: Colloid osmotic pressure relates to edema, not to how stasis causes thrombosis.
x.3: Lower coagulation proteins would reduce, not increase, clotting.

m.1: mixes up stasis and turbulence effects

items.q: A nurse states that arterial thrombosis is more common than venous thrombosis because arterial blood flows rapidly.
items.w: False. Venous thrombi are the MOST common type. Arterial thrombosis is LESS common precisely because of the rapid blood flow and the thick elastic arterial wall that resists injury. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II), slide exercise)

x.0: Venous thrombi are most common; rapid arterial flow protects arteries.

m.0: thinks arterial thrombi are most common

items.q: A client is recovering from hip surgery and has a deep vein thrombosis in the femoral vein. Which complication should the nurse monitor for most closely?
o: Embolization to the lungs causing pulmonary infarction
Embolization to the brain causing a stroke
items.w: Deep vein thrombi form in the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins, mainly through stasis and hypercoagulability after surgery or immobility. Their important complication is embolization to the lungs: about 95% of pulmonary emboli come from DVT, causing pulmonary infarction, hemorrhage or sudden death depending on size. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Systemic emboli to the brain come from the left heart or arteries; venous emboli reach the lungs unless there is a septal defect.
x.2: Fat embolism follows long bone fracture, not venous thrombosis.
x.3: Cholesterol emboli come from ruptured atheromatous plaques.

m.1: sends venous emboli to the systemic circulation

items.q: A nurse reviews clients with cardiac thrombi. Match each type of cardiac thrombus to its usual setting.

choices: Left atrial appendage in mitral stenosis
Left ventricular wall over a myocardial infarct
Heart valves in rheumatic fever, SLE or bacterial endocarditis

items.w: Cardiac thrombi form in chambers and on valves. In mitral stenosis, stasis in the dilated left atrium produces an auricular thrombus over the appendage. Over a myocardial infarct, the damaged left ventricular endocardium carries a mural thrombus. On valves, thrombi appear as vegetations in rheumatic fever, systemic lupus erythematosus and bacterial endocarditis. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.3: The popliteal vein is a site of deep vein thrombosis, not a cardiac thrombus.

m.3: confuses venous and cardiac thrombi

rs.0: A client with mitral stenosis has an auricular thrombus. Where should the nurse expect it to form?
rs.1: A client recovering from a myocardial infarction develops a mural thrombus. Where does it form?
rs.2: A client's echocardiogram shows vegetations. Where are these thrombi located?

items.q: A client's old thrombus is examined and shows ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts with new capillary channels. Which fate of a thrombus is this?
items.w: Thrombi have four fates. Recent thrombi can dissolve by fibrinolysis. They can propagate, adding platelets and fibrin and forming a tail that is liable to detach. They can embolize. Older thrombi become organized by ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, and capillary channels form that re-establish the lumen (recanalization). (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Dissolution is rapid shrinkage and disappearance of a RECENT thrombus by fibrinolysis.
x.2: Propagation is growth of the thrombus by adding platelets and fibrin, forming a tail.
x.3: Embolization is detachment of the thrombus from the vessel wall.

m.1: mixes up dissolution and organization

items.q: A nurse explains why a growing thrombus with a long tail is dangerous. What happens during propagation?
o: The thrombus adds platelets and fibrin, forming a tail that is more liable to detach and embolize.
Fibrinolysis shrinks the thrombus until it disappears.
Fibroblasts grow in and form new channels through it.
The thrombus becomes infected and produces pyemia.
items.w: Propagation means the thrombus keeps accumulating platelets and fibrin. The tail that forms is more liable to detach, so propagation sets up embolization. Infected venous thrombi (thrombophlebitis) are the source of septic emboli that produce pyemia. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: That is dissolution.
x.2: That is organization and recanalization.
x.3: Septic thrombi produce pyemia when they embolize; that is not propagation.

m.1: mixes up propagation and dissolution

items.q: A client on bed rest after surgery suddenly develops dyspnea, and pulmonary embolism is suspected. Which is the most likely source of the embolus?
o: A thrombus in the deep veins of the legs
A mural thrombus in the left ventricle
An ulcerated atheromatous plaque in the aorta
items.w: A pulmonary embolus starts in a systemic vein and lodges in the pulmonary arteries. In 95% of cases it originates from deep vein thrombi of the legs, and it is seen in up to 25-30% of patients with DVT. Emboli from the left heart or arteries travel instead to systemic organs. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II), slide note (why venous thrombi are most common))

x.1: Left heart thrombi enter the systemic circulation, giving systemic emboli.
x.2: Aortic plaques give systemic or cholesterol emboli, not pulmonary emboli.
x.3: Mitral vegetations embolize into the systemic arterial circulation.

m.1: sends left-heart emboli to the lungs

items.q: A nurse teaching about deep vein thrombosis states that about 95% of pulmonary emboli originate from thrombi in the deep veins of the legs.
items.w: True. In 95% of cases pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombi of the legs, and pulmonary embolism is observed in up to 25-30% of patients with DVT. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: This statement is true: 95% of pulmonary emboli come from leg DVT.

items.q: A nurse reviews the outcomes of pulmonary embolism by embolus size. Match each embolus to its usual outcome.

rows: Large saddle embolus at the pulmonary bifurcation
Medium embolus in a normal lung
Medium embolus in a congested lung
choices: Sudden death from acute right-sided failure
Clinically silent with no effect ever

items.w: The effect of a pulmonary embolus depends on its size and on the lung. 60-80% are small and clinically silent. A large saddle embolus at the bifurcation or in a main pulmonary artery causes sudden death from acute right-sided failure. A medium embolus causes only hemorrhage in a normal lung, but infarction in a congested lung. Small repeated emboli cause pulmonary hypertension and right-sided failure (cor pulmonale). (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.4: 60-80% of emboli are small and silent, but none of these listed emboli is silent.

items.q: A client recovering from a large anterior myocardial infarction develops a cold, pulseless leg. Which source of the arterial embolus is most likely?
o: An intracardiac thrombus over the infarcted left ventricular wall
A deep vein thrombus of the leg
A fat embolus from bone marrow
items.w: Systemic emboli travel in the arterial circulation. About 80% arise from intracardiac thrombi, two thirds of which are associated with left ventricular wall infarcts. Others come from aortic aneurysms, ulcerated atheromatous plaques or paradoxical emboli. About 75% lodge in the lower extremities and 10% in the brain. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Leg vein thrombi travel to the lungs unless they pass through a septal defect.
x.2: Fat emboli follow long bone fractures.
x.3: Amniotic fluid embolism occurs during delivery.

m.1: sends venous emboli to the systemic circulation

items.q: A client with an interatrial septal defect and a known leg DVT suddenly develops stroke symptoms. Which type of embolism best explains this?
items.w: A paradoxical embolus begins as a venous embolus, but instead of reaching the lungs it crosses an interatrial or interventricular defect into the systemic circulation. A leg vein thrombus can therefore reach the brain in a client with a septal defect. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: A pulmonary embolus lodges in the lung, not the brain.
x.2: Fat embolism follows long bone fracture or soft tissue trauma.
x.3: Atheroembolism discharges debris from a ruptured arterial plaque.

m.1: sends a crossed embolus to the lungs

items.q: Two days after a femoral shaft fracture, a client becomes tachypneic, dyspneic, tachycardic and confused, and labs show thrombocytopenia and anemia. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.w: Fat embolism occurs in about 90% of people with severe skeletal injuries, most commonly long bone fractures, but fewer than 10% develop clinical findings. The syndrome begins 1-3 days after injury with tachypnea, dyspnea and tachycardia, neurologic symptoms, and thrombocytopenia and anemia. Fat globules obstruct vessels mechanically and free fatty acids injure endothelium and activate platelets; it is fatal in 5-15%. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Air embolism follows entry of more than 100 cc of air, as in neck vein or chest wall injury.
x.2: Amniotic fluid embolism occurs during delivery.
x.3: Cholesterol emboli come from atheromatous plaques.

m.1: mixes up fat and air emboli

items.q: A nurse reviews situations that carry a risk of air embolism. Which situations apply? Select all that apply.
o: Air trapped in a coronary artery during bypass surgery
items.w: Gas bubbles in the circulation coalesce into frothy masses that obstruct flow and cause distal ischemia. Causes include injury to large neck veins, chest wall injury, obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, air trapped in a coronary artery during bypass surgery, and decompression sickness (Caisson disease). (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II), slide exercise (decompression sickness))

x.5: Long bone fracture is the most common cause of FAT embolism.
x.6: This lets amniotic fluid enter the maternal circulation: amniotic fluid embolism.
x.7: Plaque rupture discharges cholesterol debris: atheroembolism.

m.5: mixes up fat and air emboli

items.q: A nurse states that more than 100 cc of air is required to have a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation.
items.w: True. Air embolism needs more than 100 cc of air to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: This statement is true: more than 100 cc of air is needed.

items.q: During delivery, a client suddenly develops severe dyspnea, cyanosis, shock and a seizure, followed by bleeding from IV sites. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
o: Air embolism from a neck vein injury
items.w: Amniotic fluid or fetal tissue can enter the maternal circulation through a tear in the placental membranes or ruptured uterine veins. It causes sudden severe dyspnea, cyanosis and shock, neurologic impairment (headache, seizures, coma), pulmonary edema and DIC. It is rare (1 in 40,000 deliveries) but has 80% mortality, and 85% of survivors keep a neurologic deficit. (Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II))

x.1: Fat embolism begins 1-3 days after a long bone fracture.
x.2: PE from DVT does not explain the seizure and DIC at delivery.
x.3: There is no neck vein injury; air embolism needs over 100 cc of air.

m.1: mixes up amniotic and fat emboli

items.q: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of malaise and chest pain. Three weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved without treatment. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). Examination shows several subcutaneous nodules on her elbows and wrist bilaterally and a new-onset early systolic murmur best heard at the apex in the left lateral position. An endomyocardial biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?
items.w: A sore throat 3 weeks earlier, fever, subcutaneous nodules and a new apical murmur fit acute rheumatic fever. Its pathognomonic microscopic lesion is the Aschoff body, found in all layers of the heart: foci of necrosis with T lymphocytes and Anitschkow cells, which are activated macrophages (cardiac histiocytes). The valve vegetations overlie foci of fibrinoid necrosis. A biopsy therefore shows fibrinoid necrosis with a histiocytic infiltrate. (The slide's word "endomysial" is corrected here to endomyocardial.) (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever), in-class case)

x.1: This pattern is not the lesion of rheumatic carditis, which is the Aschoff body (focal necrosis, T lymphocytes and Anitschkow histiocytes).
x.2: Misfolded protein deposits are not part of the rheumatic lesion described in ARF.
x.3: Eosinophilic protein infiltration is not part of the rheumatic lesion described in ARF.
x.4: Fibrosis follows healing in chronic disease; myofibrillar disarray is not part of the ARF lesion.

m.1: expects infarct-type necrosis in ARF

items.q: A 9-year-old boy from Eritrea is admitted to the hospital for lethargy and increased work of breathing. He has had recurrent episodes of fever, shortness of breath, and fatigue over the past 3 years. His pulse is 132/min and blood pressure is 90/66 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 82%. Auscultation of the chest shows coarse crackles in both lungs and a diastolic murmur at the cardiac apex. Despite appropriate lifesaving measures, he dies. A photomicrograph of a section of myocardium obtained at autopsy is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's cardiac disease?
items.w: Recurrent febrile episodes, pulmonary congestion and an apical diastolic murmur (mitral stenosis) in a child from an endemic area point to rheumatic heart disease, and the autopsy section shows Aschoff bodies. The disease is immunologically mediated: antibodies and CD4+ T cells raised against streptococcal M proteins cross-react with self antigens in the heart. Antibodies binding tissue antigens activate complement and recruit macrophages, which is a type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction; the slide states the antibody cross-reaction but not the term "type II". (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever), in-class case)

x.1: Amastigote infiltration means direct parasitic invasion of the myocardium, not the antibody cross-reaction of rheumatic heart disease.
x.2: Rheumatic carditis is not caused by a toxin; it is caused by antibodies and T cells cross-reacting with heart antigens.
x.3: Caseating granulomas are not the lesion of rheumatic heart disease; the Aschoff body is.

m.2: thinks strep toxin damages the heart directly

items.q: A group of epidemiologists is studying the rates of cardiac surgeries performed in several Southeast Asian countries compared to the United States. Results show a significant increase in the number of mitral valve replacements performed in Vietnam in adults aged 30–50 years compared to the same age group in the United States. Which of the following public health interventions is most likely to decrease this number?
o: Prompt antibiotic treatment for bacterial pharyngitis
Improved access to drug rehabilitation centers
Genetic screening program for FBN1 gene mutation
Screening echocardiography for prolapsed anterior mitral valve leaflets
items.w: Mitral valve replacement in young adults in a developing country points to chronic rheumatic heart disease, which follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by decades. The incidence and mortality of rheumatic fever fell over the past century because of better socioeconomic conditions and rapid diagnosis and treatment of strep pharyngitis. Prompt antibiotic treatment prevents the immune reaction and therefore the valve scarring. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever), in-class case)

x.1: Drug rehabilitation addresses IV drug use endocarditis, which mainly affects the tricuspid valve.
x.2: FBN1 mutation screening is unrelated to rheumatic valve disease, the cause described here.
x.3: Diphtheria vaccination does not prevent group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
x.4: Screening finds valve disease; it does not prevent rheumatic scarring.

m.1: links mitral disease to IV drug use

items.q: A nurse takes the history of a child with suspected acute rheumatic fever. Which history is most consistent with the diagnosis?
o: An 8-year-old with a sore throat caused by group A streptococci 3 weeks ago
A 40-year-old with a sore throat 3 weeks ago
An 8-year-old with a sore throat 2 days ago
An 8-year-old with a group A streptococcal skin infection 6 months ago
items.w: Acute rheumatic fever appears 10 days to 6 weeks after group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis, develops in about 3% of infected patients and is most common in children aged 5-15. The delay reflects the time needed for antibodies and T cells against streptococcal M proteins to form and cross-react with heart antigens. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: ARF occurs most often in children aged 5-15.
x.2: ARF appears 10 days to 6 weeks after the pharyngitis, not within 2 days.
x.3: ARF follows streptococcal PHARYNGITIS by 10 days to 6 weeks.

m.1: ignores the age pattern
m.2: ignores the latent period

items.q: A pathology report on a child's heart describes macrophages with abundant cytoplasm and a central nucleus whose chromatin forms a slender wavy ribbon. What are these cells?
items.w: Anitschkow cells (caterpillar cells) are cardiac histiocytes: macrophages with abundant cytoplasm and central round to oval nuclei whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon. Together with focal necrosis and T lymphocytes they form the Aschoff body, the pathognomonic lesion of acute rheumatic fever found in all layers of the heart. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in chronic pulmonary congestion.
x.2: Foam cells are lipid-filled cells in atherosclerotic lesions.
x.3: T lymphocytes are also in the Aschoff body, but they lack the caterpillar chromatin pattern.

m.1: mixes up heart failure cells and Anitschkow cells
m.2: mixes up foam cells and Anitschkow cells

items.q: A nurse auscultates a pericardial friction rub in a child with acute rheumatic fever. Which pericardial lesion is expected?
o: Vegetations along the lines of valve closure
items.w: Acute rheumatic fever causes a pancarditis with Aschoff bodies in all layers. In the pericardium it causes fibrinous inflammation, the "bread and butter" pericarditis that produces a friction rub. The myocardium shows myocarditis and the valves show small vegetations along the lines of closure. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: Vegetations are the lesion of rheumatic ENDOcarditis, on the valves.
x.2: Brown induration is fibrosis of the lung in chronic congestion.
x.3: A mural thrombus forms in the left ventricle over an infarct.

m.1: puts valve lesions in the pericardium

items.q: A child's echocardiogram during acute rheumatic fever shows small vegetations along the lines of valve closure. Which valve is most commonly affected?
items.w: Rheumatic vegetations are small, lie along the lines of closure and overlie foci of fibrinoid necrosis. They favor the high-pressure valves: mitral (65%) and aortic (25%). Chronic rheumatic heart disease follows the same pattern, with the mitral valve most affected. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: The aortic valve is second (25%).
x.2: The tricuspid valve is typical of IV drug use endocarditis, not rheumatic fever.
x.3: The pulmonary valve is not among the most common sites.

m.1: ranks aortic first
m.2: confuses RHD with IVDU endocarditis

items.q: A nurse reviews a child's findings using the Jones criteria. Which findings are MAJOR criteria? Select all that apply.
items.w: The Jones major criteria are carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. The minor criteria are fever, arthralgia, previous rheumatic fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation (ESR, CRP, leukocytosis) and ECG changes (prolonged PR interval). (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.5: Fever is a minor criterion.
x.6: Arthralgia (joint pain without arthritis) is a minor criterion.
x.7: A prolonged PR interval is a minor criterion.

m.5: mixes up major and minor Jones criteria
m.7: mixes up major and minor Jones criteria

items.q: A child has Sydenham chorea, fever and a raised ESR, and the streptococcal antibody titer is elevated. How should the nurse interpret these findings using the Jones criteria?
o: The criteria are met: 1 major and 2 minor criteria with evidence of preceding strep infection.
The criteria are not met because 2 major criteria are always required.
The criteria are not met because chorea is a minor criterion.
The criteria are met even without evidence of streptococcal infection.
items.w: Acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed with 2 major criteria, or 1 major and 2 minor criteria, supported by evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection (positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or a raised or rising antibody titer). Chorea is major; fever and a raised ESR are minor; the elevated titer is the supporting evidence. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: Diagnosis needs 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor criteria.
x.2: Sydenham chorea is a MAJOR criterion.
x.3: The criteria must be supported by evidence of preceding group A strep infection; here the titer supplies it.

m.1: forgets the 1 major + 2 minor rule
m.2: mixes up major and minor Jones criteria

items.q: A nurse tells a family that the migratory polyarthritis of acute rheumatic fever typically leaves chronic joint deformities.
items.w: False. Migratory ("fleeting") polyarthritis of the large joints is self-limited and leaves NO chronic deformities. The lasting damage of rheumatic fever is to the heart valves. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.0: The arthritis is self-limited with no chronic deformities.

items.q: A client has long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis. Which consequences should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Left atrial dilatation with possible thrombi
Chronic venous congestion of the lungs
items.w: A fibrotic "fish mouth" mitral valve obstructs flow from the left atrium, which dilates and may harbor thrombi that embolize. Back pressure causes chronic pulmonary venous congestion, lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and eventually chronic right-sided failure. Atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism and infective endocarditis complicate it. The left ventricle, upstream of nothing that is blocked, is largely unaffected. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.5: The left ventricle is largely unaffected by isolated pure mitral stenosis.

m.5: thinks mitral stenosis enlarges the LV

items.q: A nurse explains that chronic rheumatic heart disease usually becomes clinically manifest decades after the episode of acute rheumatic fever.
items.w: True. ARF endocarditis heals by fibrosis, repeated infections reactivate it, and the chronic valve scarring usually becomes clinically manifest after decades. (Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever))

x.1: This statement is true: RHD usually appears decades later.

items.q: A nurse reviews vessel biopsy reports. Match each pattern of arteriosclerosis to its description.

choices: Intimal atheromas that protrude into the lumen
Calcific deposits in muscular arteries after age 50
Arteriolar wall thickened by amorphous proteinaceous material
Fatty spots of foam cells under 1 mm

items.w: Arteriosclerosis means thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls, in three patterns. Atherosclerosis, the most frequent and important, forms intimal atheromas. Mönckeberg medial sclerosis lays down calcific deposits in muscular arteries of people over 50. Arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles in hypertension and diabetes: the hyaline type deposits amorphous protein in the wall, and the hyperplastic type shows onion-skinning that narrows the lumen. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.4: Fatty spots are the earliest lesion OF atherosclerosis, not a separate pattern.

items.q: A nurse explains that Mönckeberg medial sclerosis mainly affects arterioles in clients with hypertension.
items.w: False. Mönckeberg medial sclerosis is calcific deposits in MUSCULAR ARTERIES in people older than 50. The pattern that affects small arteries and arterioles in hypertension and diabetes is arteriolosclerosis. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.0: Mönckeberg affects muscular arteries; arteriolosclerosis affects arterioles.

items.q: A nurse counsels a client about atherosclerosis risk. Which risk factors can the client modify? Select all that apply.
items.w: Atherosclerosis risk factors are split into non-modifiable (increasing age, male gender, genetic abnormalities and family history) and modifiable (hyperlipidemia, especially hypercholesterolemia with high LDL, hypertension, cigarette smoking and diabetes mellitus). Counseling targets the modifiable ones. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.4: Age is a non-modifiable risk factor.
x.5: Male gender is a non-modifiable risk factor.
x.6: Genetic abnormalities and family history are non-modifiable.

m.4: thinks non-modifiable factors are modifiable
m.5: thinks non-modifiable factors are modifiable

items.q: A nurse explains how an atheroma develops according to the response-to-injury hypothesis. Arrange the steps in order.
o: Endothelial dysfunction with monocyte adhesion and emigration
Smooth muscle recruitment to the intima and macrophage activation
Macrophages and smooth muscle cells engulf lipid to form foam cells (fatty streak)
Smooth muscle proliferation with collagen and ECM deposition (fibrofatty atheroma)
items.w: The response-to-injury hypothesis sees atherosclerosis as a chronic inflammatory response to endothelial injury. Injury from hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, homocysteine, toxins, viruses or immune reactions makes the endothelium leaky and sticky, so monocytes adhere and migrate in. Smooth muscle cells are recruited into the intima and macrophages activate; both engulf lipid as foam cells, forming a fatty streak. Smooth muscle proliferation and collagen deposition then build the fibrofatty atheroma. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

items.q: A biopsy of a young client's aorta shows flat yellow lesions about 1 cm long made of foam cells that do not narrow the lumen. Which lesion is this?
items.w: Atherosclerotic lesions progress from fatty spots (multiple yellow spots under 1 mm made of foam cells) to fatty streaks, where spots coalesce into elongated streaks 1 cm or longer. Streaks contain foam cells and a little extracellular lipid, are not significantly raised and do not disturb blood flow. Atheromas come later. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.1: Fatty spots are smaller (less than 1 mm) and are the earliest lesion.
x.2: An atheroma is a RAISED patch with a lipid core under a fibrous cap.
x.3: Mönckeberg sclerosis is calcification of the media of muscular arteries.

m.1: mixes up spots and streaks
m.2: calls any fatty lesion a plaque

items.q: A nurse reviews the gross description of a coronary atheroma. Which description is accurate?
o: A raised intimal patch with a soft yellow lipid core covered by a firm white fibrous cap
A flat yellow streak that does not disturb blood flow
Calcific deposits in the media of a muscular artery
A thickened arteriolar wall with onion-skinning
items.w: An atheroma is a raised patch within the intima with a soft, yellow core of lipid covered by a firm, white fibrous cap. Microscopically it has cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages, other leukocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibers, proteoglycans) and intracellular and extracellular lipid. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.1: That describes a fatty streak.
x.2: That describes Mönckeberg medial sclerosis.
x.3: That describes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

m.1: mixes up streaks and plaques

items.q: A nurse states that fatty streaks are not significantly raised and do not disturb blood flow.
items.w: True. Fatty streaks are elongated streaks 1 cm or longer that are not significantly raised and do not cause any disturbance in blood flow. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.1: This statement is true: fatty streaks are flat and do not disturb flow.

items.q: A nurse reviews where atherosclerosis most often develops. Which sites are common? Select all that apply.
o: Vessels of the circle of Willis
items.w: Atheromas form in large and medium arteries. The common sites listed are the lower abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries and the vessels of the circle of Willis, which explains the main consequences: ischemic heart disease, stroke, aortic aneurysm and peripheral vascular disease. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.5: Arterioles are affected by arteriolosclerosis, not atherosclerosis.
x.6: Leg veins are a site of deep vein thrombosis, not atherosclerosis.

m.5: mixes up atherosclerosis and arteriolosclerosis sites

items.q: A client with known coronary atherosclerosis suddenly develops an acute myocardial infarction. Which plaque change most likely triggered the event?
o: Rupture or erosion of the plaque surface, which induces thrombosis
Formation of a new fatty streak
Mönckeberg medial sclerosis of the artery
items.w: Acute plaque changes are rupture, ulceration or erosion of the luminal surface, which induces thrombosis, and fissure with hemorrhage into the plaque, which can expand or rupture it. Plaque rupture can also discharge debris (atheroembolism). Thrombosis on a ruptured coronary plaque is what turns chronic ischemic disease into infarction. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.1: Calcification is a chronic change of atheromas, not the acute trigger of thrombosis.
x.2: Fatty streaks are flat early lesions that do not disturb flow.
x.3: Mönckeberg sclerosis is medial calcification, a separate pattern.

m.1: thinks calcification causes acute events

items.q: A nurse explains the clinical consequences of atherosclerosis at different sites. Match each site to its major consequence.

choices: Peripheral vascular disease with gangrene of the legs

items.w: Where an atheroma narrows or thromboses an artery decides the disease. Coronary atherosclerosis causes ischemic heart disease, cerebral atherosclerosis causes stroke, aortic atherosclerosis weakens the media and causes aneurysms, and atherosclerosis of the limb arteries causes peripheral vascular disease and gangrene. (Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis))

x.4: Pulmonary infarction follows pulmonary embolism, usually from DVT, not atherosclerosis.

m.4: links PE to atherosclerosis

rs.2: A client has advanced aortic atherosclerosis. Which consequence should the nurse anticipate?

items.q: A 52-year-old client's average blood pressure over several visits is 132/82 mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this reading?
o: It meets the definition of hypertension.
It is normal because hypertension starts at 140/90 mm Hg.
It is hypertension only if the systolic reading is 140 or more.
It cannot be classified without a renin level.
items.w: Both the ACC/AHA (2023) and the Saudi Heart Association define hypertension as a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or higher. A reading of 132/82 is above both numbers. Hypertension affects 1 in 3 US adults and is more common with age and obesity. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: The current definition (ACC/AHA 2023 and SHA) is 130/80 mm Hg or higher.
x.2: Either value at or above 130/80 meets the definition; 132/82 exceeds both.
x.3: Hypertension is defined by blood pressure, not by renin.

m.1: uses the old 140/90 threshold

items.q: A nurse reviews a client's antihypertensive medication list. Match each drug to its class.
items.w: The drug list groups antihypertensives by where they act: diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, furosemide, spironolactone), sympathoplegic drugs (clonidine, methyldopa, prazosin, propranolol, labetalol, esmolol), vasodilators (hydralazine, nitroprusside, minoxidil, diazoxide, fenoldopam, CCBs) and inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system: ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, enalaprilat), ARBs (losartan) and renin inhibitors (aliskiren). (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension), drug list slide)

x.4: ACE inhibitors on the list are captopril, enalapril and enalaprilat.
x.5: The only renin inhibitor is aliskiren.

m.4: mixes up ARBs and ACE inhibitors

rs.1: A client's medication list includes clonidine. Which drug class should the nurse identify?
rs.2: A client receives hydralazine for blood pressure. Which drug class does it belong to?
rs.3: A client who could not tolerate captopril is switched to losartan. Which drug class is losartan?

items.q: A client who has taken a thiazide for 6 weeks asks why the blood pressure stays down even though urination is back to normal. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
o: Peripheral vascular resistance has fallen because body sodium depletion lowers calcium in vascular smooth muscle.
Plasma volume and cardiac output stay reduced for as long as the drug is taken.
The thiazide blocks L-type calcium channels in the arterioles.
The thiazide blocks beta-1 receptors on the heart.
items.w: Diuretics first lower blood pressure by reducing plasma volume and cardiac output. After 4-8 weeks of therapy volume and output return toward normal, but peripheral vascular resistance falls through arteriolar vasodilation. The likely main mechanism is depletion of body Na+ stores: less Na+ in smooth muscle lowers intracellular Ca++ through the Na/Ca exchanger. Renal prostaglandins and K channel opening may also contribute. This is why diuretic efficacy does not strictly match antihypertensive efficacy. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Volume and cardiac output return toward normal after 4-8 weeks; the early effect does not persist.
x.2: Blocking L-type Ca++ channels is the mechanism of calcium channel blockers.
x.3: Beta-1 blockade is the mechanism of beta blockers.

m.1: thinks diuretics work only by volume loss

items.q: A client with chronic kidney disease has hypertension that needs a diuretic. Which diuretic class should the nurse anticipate?
o: A loop diuretic such as furosemide
items.w: Thiazides and thiazide-like drugs are the first-choice antihypertensive diuretics and the most effective in patients with normal renal function. Loop diuretics are preferable only in specific situations such as malignant hypertension and concomitant chronic kidney disease. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Thiazides are first choice in patients with NORMAL renal function.
x.2: Potassium-sparing diuretics are used only combined with thiazides to counteract hypokalemia.
x.3: Diazoxide is a potassium channel opener that does not cause diuresis.

m.1: uses thiazides in CKD
m.2: thinks K-sparing diuretics are used alone

items.q: A client on hydrochlorothiazide has a low serum potassium. Which drug should the nurse anticipate being added?
items.w: Potassium-sparing diuretics are used only in combination with thiazides, to counteract the hypokalemia thiazides cause. Spironolactone is the potassium-sparing diuretic on the list and is also used for hypertension due to hyperaldosteronism. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Furosemide is a loop diuretic; it would not correct hypokalemia.
x.2: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic, which also lowers potassium.
x.3: Fenoldopam is an IV D1 agonist that itself decreases serum potassium.

m.1: adds a K-wasting diuretic

items.q: A nurse explains that the antihypertensive doses of thiazides are lower than those required for a diuretic effect.
items.w: True. Thiazides lower blood pressure at doses lower than those needed for diuresis, another sign that they do not work only by increasing urine output. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: This statement is true: antihypertensive doses are lower than diuretic doses.

items.q: A client starts nifedipine for hypertension. Which change in heart rate should the nurse expect?
o: Heart rate will fall and AV block will develop.
Marked postural drops in heart rate will occur.
items.w: Dihydropyridines such as nifedipine block Ca++ channels in the vessels only, so they lower peripheral resistance and heart rate (and cardiac output) may increase. Verapamil and diltiazem also block cardiac channels, so heart rate is unchanged or decreased. All CCBs lower peripheral resistance with negligible postural hypotension. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Unchanged or decreased heart rate is the pattern of verapamil and diltiazem.

items.q: A nurse reviews the pharmacology of calcium channel blockers. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They bind L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channels from the inner side of the membrane.
Verapamil and diltiazem block Ca++ channels in both heart and vessels.
Dihydropyridines block Ca++ channels in the vessels only.
Their blockade can be partly reversed by beta-1 agonists.
Short-acting nifedipine is preferred for long-term hypertension.
items.w: Calcium channel blockers bind the L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channel from the inner side of the membrane. Verapamil and diltiazem (low vascular selectivity) block channels in heart and vessels, while dihydropyridines (nifedipine high, nicardipine very high selectivity) act only on vessels. Drugs that increase Ca++ flux, such as beta-1 agonists, can partly reverse the blockade. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.4: Nicardipine has VERY HIGH vascular selectivity; verapamil and diltiazem have low selectivity.
x.5: Short-acting nifedipine has been linked to increased mortality in hypertension.

m.5: thinks short-acting nifedipine is safe

items.q: A client is admitted with a hypertensive emergency. Which calcium channel blocker should the nurse anticipate?
items.w: Calcium channel blockers are first-choice drugs in hypertension and are more effective in African patients. For hypertensive emergencies nicardipine is used. Long-term studies have linked short-acting nifedipine to increased mortality, whereas slow-release formulations apparently do not increase the risk. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Verapamil is not the CCB named for hypertensive emergencies; it also blocks cardiac channels.
x.3: Diltiazem is not the CCB named for hypertensive emergencies.

items.q: A nurse states that short-acting nifedipine is preferred for long-term hypertension because it lowers mortality.
items.w: False. Long-term epidemiological studies report an INCREASED risk of mortality with short-acting nifedipine in hypertension; slow-release formulations apparently do not increase this risk. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

items.q: A client is started on aliskiren. Which laboratory pattern should the nurse expect?
o: Decreased angiotensin II and aldosterone with increased renin concentration
Increased angiotensin II with decreased renin
Decreased renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone
Increased bradykinin with unchanged angiotensin II
items.w: Aliskiren, the only renin inhibitor on the market, competitively inhibits renin, the enzyme that converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I (the rate-limiting step). Angiotensin I, angiotensin II and aldosterone fall, and with less negative feedback the renin level rises. It is usually well tolerated but can cause hyperkalemia when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Renin concentration increases, not decreases.
x.3: Raised bradykinin is an effect of ACE inhibitors.

m.2: thinks renin falls with a renin inhibitor
m.3: mixes up renin and ACE inhibitors

items.q: A client taking captopril reports a dry, irritating cough. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: Accumulation of bradykinin, prostaglandins or substance P in the lungs
Accumulation of angiotensin II in the lungs
Blockade of beta-2 receptors in the airways
items.w: The converting enzyme both forms angiotensin II and inactivates bradykinin. Inhibiting it lowers angiotensin II and raises bradykinin. The dry, disturbing cough may be mediated by accumulation in the lungs of bradykinin and prostaglandins or, more likely, substance P. ARBs have no effect on bradykinin, which is why they are the alternative. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: ACE inhibitors DECREASE angiotensin II formation.
x.2: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II-driven aldosterone; aldosterone does not cause cough.
x.3: Bronchoconstriction from beta blockade is a beta-blocker effect.

m.3: mixes up ACE inhibitor cough and beta-blocker bronchospasm

items.q: A client is started on enalapril. Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.

They are pregnancy category D. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.5: ACE inhibitors cause HYPERkalemia.
x.6: Hypertrichosis is an adverse effect of minoxidil.
x.7: A positive Coombs' test is caused by methyldopa.

items.q: A client who started lisinopril last week reports swelling of the lips and tongue. Which action should the nurse take first?

Reassure the client that this is the common ACE inhibitor cough.
Tell the client it happens only after the first dose and will settle.
Advise taking the next dose with food.
items.w: Angioneurotic edema is a rare adverse effect of ACE inhibitors (up to 0.3%) but it may be fatal; inhibition of bradykinin metabolism may be involved. Swelling of the lips and tongue therefore needs immediate action, unlike the common dry cough. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: First-dose hypotension, not angioedema, is the effect linked to initial doses.
x.3: Taking the drug with food does nothing for angioedema.

m.2: confuses angioedema with first-dose hypotension

items.q: A client has liver disease and needs an ACE inhibitor. Which ACE inhibitor must be activated by the liver before it works?
items.w: Captopril, lisinopril and enalaprilat are active drugs. All other ACE inhibitors (enalapril, benazepril, fosinopril and others) are prodrugs that the liver converts into active metabolites. Enalaprilat is also the only one given intravenously. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Lisinopril is an active drug and needs no activation.

items.q: A client in a hypertensive emergency needs an ACE inhibitor intravenously. Which drug should the nurse anticipate?
items.w: All ACE inhibitors except enalaprilat are given by the oral route only. Enalaprilat, the active form of enalapril, is given IV and is the ACE inhibitor used in hypertensive emergencies. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Enalapril is an oral prodrug.
x.2: Captopril is given by mouth only.
x.3: Losartan is an ARB given by mouth only.

items.q: A pregnant client at 20 weeks has hypertension. Which drug orders should the nurse question? Select all that apply.
items.w: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are pregnancy category D; ARBs carry a substantial teratogenic risk. Orders for losartan or enalapril in pregnancy should be questioned. Methyldopa is often preferred in pregnancy, and labetalol is used for hypertension in pregnancy. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Methyldopa is often preferred in pregnancy; long experience shows it is not harmful to the fetus.
x.3: Labetalol is used to treat hypertension in pregnancy.

m.2: thinks methyldopa is unsafe in pregnancy
m.3: thinks labetalol is unsafe in pregnancy

items.q: A client who developed a cough on captopril is switched to losartan. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?
o: "Losartan blocks the angiotensin receptor, so it should not cause the same cough."
"Losartan works the same way as captopril by blocking the converting enzyme."
"Losartan raises bradykinin even more than captopril."
"Losartan is safe if I become pregnant."
items.w: Losartan competitively and selectively blocks AT1 receptors. It prevents or reverses most actions of angiotensin II and inhibits them more completely than ACE inhibitors, because enzymes other than ACE can still make angiotensin II. It has no effect on bradykinin, so it does not cause the bradykinin-related cough, which makes it the alternative to ACE inhibitors. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Losartan blocks AT1 receptors; it does not inhibit ACE.
x.2: ARBs have no effect on bradykinin metabolism.
x.3: ARBs are pregnancy category D with substantial teratogenic risk.

m.1: thinks ARBs inhibit ACE
m.3: thinks ARBs are safe in pregnancy

items.q: A nurse states that losartan lowers blood pressure by inhibiting the converting enzyme that forms angiotensin II.
items.w: False. Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor antagonist: it competitively blocks AT1 receptors. Inhibiting the converting enzyme is the mechanism of ACE inhibitors such as captopril. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.0: Losartan blocks AT1 receptors; ACE inhibitors block the enzyme.

items.q: A client with diabetes and early glomerular disease is prescribed an ACE inhibitor. How does the drug slow progression of the kidney disease?
o: It prevents angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction of the efferent glomerular arteriole.
It dilates the afferent arteriole by releasing nitric oxide.
It increases aldosterone to retain sodium.
It blocks D1 receptors in the renal vessels.
items.w: In diabetic glomerulopathy and hypertensive nephroangiosclerosis, ACE inhibitors decrease disease progression by preventing angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction of the efferent glomerular arteriole. They are also first-choice in hypertension and are used after myocardial infarction and in chronic heart failure. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Nitric oxide release is the mechanism of nitroprusside.
x.2: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II-driven aldosterone secretion.
x.3: Fenoldopam ACTIVATES D1 receptors; ACE inhibitors do not act on them.

items.q: A pregnant client needs treatment for chronic hypertension. Which drug is often preferred because long experience shows it is not harmful to the fetus?
items.w: Methyldopa is taken up by adrenergic neurons and converted to methylnorepinephrine, which activates central alpha-2 receptors and lowers sympathetic tone. It is a second-choice drug in general, but it is often preferred for hypertension in pregnancy because long experience shows it does not harm the fetus. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Losartan is pregnancy category D with substantial teratogenic risk.
x.2: ACE inhibitors are pregnancy category D.
x.3: Minoxidil is reserved for severe resistant hypertension because of its toxicity.

m.2: thinks ACE inhibitors are safe in pregnancy

items.q: A client taking clonidine plans to stop the drug suddenly because it causes drowsiness. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: "Stopping clonidine suddenly can cause a hypertensive crisis, so talk with your provider before stopping."
"Stopping suddenly is safe because clonidine has no withdrawal effects."
"Drowsiness means the dose is too low; take an extra tablet."
"Clonidine only causes problems when given through the skin."
items.w: Clonidine and methyldopa lower central adrenergic tone. Their CNS adverse effects include sedation and drowsiness, and clonidine (rarely methyldopa) can cause a hypertensive crisis when suddenly withdrawn. The client should not stop it abruptly. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Sedation and drowsiness are adverse effects, not a sign of under-dosing.
x.3: Transdermal clonidine causes skin eruptions, but withdrawal crisis can occur with any route.

m.1: thinks clonidine can be stopped abruptly

items.q: A client on long-term methyldopa needs a blood transfusion and the crossmatch shows a problem. Which adverse effect of methyldopa explains this?
items.w: Methyldopa is a false neurotransmitter that becomes methylnorepinephrine and stimulates central alpha-2 receptors. Besides sedation and sexual dysfunction, it can cause a positive Coombs' test, which matters when blood is crossmatched. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Lupoid syndrome is an immunological adverse effect of hydralazine.
x.2: Hyperkalemia is an adverse effect of ACE inhibitors and aliskiren combinations.
x.3: Cyanide toxicity is an adverse effect of nitroprusside.

items.q: A nurse reviews how several antihypertensives act. Match each drug to its mechanism.

choices: Activates imidazoline receptors in the medulla

items.w: Methyldopa is taken up into adrenergic neurons and converted to methylnorepinephrine, an alpha-2 agonist. Clonidine activates central alpha-2 receptors and imidazoline receptors in the medulla. Both reduce central adrenergic tone. Prazosin selectively blocks alpha-1 receptors, dilating resistance and capacitance vessels. Propranolol is a non-selective beta blocker. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

items.q: A client receives the first dose of prazosin. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor for most closely?
items.w: Prazosin and doxazosin selectively block alpha-1 receptors and lower blood pressure by dilating both resistance and capacitance (venous) vessels. Dilating the veins reduces venous return on standing, so postural hypotension can occur, mainly after the first dose: the "first-dose phenomenon". Tachycardia, palpitations and syncope may accompany it. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Bronchoconstriction is an adverse effect of beta blockers.
x.2: Hypertrichosis is an adverse effect of minoxidil.
x.3: Cyanide toxicity is an adverse effect of nitroprusside.
x.4: Dry cough is an adverse effect of ACE inhibitors.

m.1: mixes up alpha and beta blocker effects

items.q: A client is started on a beta blocker for hypertension. Which adverse effects should the nurse teach the client about? Select all that apply.
items.w: Beta blockers lower heart rate and cardiac output and leave venous tone unchanged, so they do not cause postural hypotension. Adverse effects: bradycardia, hypotension and rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal; bronchoconstriction; insomnia, depression and nightmares; hypoglycemia because the liver's gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are impaired; and sexual dysfunction. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.5: Beta blockers do not cause postural hypotension because venous tone is unchanged.
x.6: Hyperglycemia is an adverse effect of diazoxide; beta blockers cause HYPOglycemia.
x.7: Hypertrichosis is an adverse effect of minoxidil.

m.5: thinks beta blockers cause postural hypotension
m.6: reverses the glucose effect of beta blockers

items.q: A client with asthma needs a beta blocker. Which drug is beta-1 selective?
items.w: Beta blockers are divided into beta-1 selective drugs (atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol) and non-selective drugs (propranolol, penbutolol, timolol). Bronchoconstriction is a respiratory adverse effect of beta blockade, so selectivity matters in a client with asthma. Labetalol and carvedilol block both alpha and beta receptors. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Propranolol is a non-selective beta blocker.
x.2: Timolol is a non-selective beta blocker.
x.3: Penbutolol is a non-selective beta blocker.
x.4: Labetalol blocks both alpha and beta receptors.

m.1: thinks propranolol is beta-1 selective

items.q: A nurse explains how a beta blocker lowers a client's blood pressure. Which explanation is accurate?
o: It decreases cardiac output and inhibits renin release by blocking beta-1 receptors.
It dilates both arterioles and veins by blocking alpha-1 receptors.
It opens potassium channels in arteriolar smooth muscle.
It lowers venous tone so blood pools on standing.
items.w: Beta blockers lower blood pressure by two beta-1 effects: blocking cardiac beta-1 receptors lowers heart rate and cardiac output, and blocking beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells inhibits renin release. Venous tone is unchanged, so they do not cause postural hypotension. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Alpha-1 blockade of resistance and capacitance vessels is how prazosin works.
x.2: Potassium channel opening is the mechanism of minoxidil and diazoxide.
x.3: Beta blockers leave venous tone unchanged and do not cause postural hypotension.

m.1: mixes up alpha and beta blocker mechanisms

items.q: A client has heart failure and hypertension. Which alpha-beta blocker is used to treat heart failure?
items.w: Labetalol and carvedilol block both alpha and beta receptors, causing vasodilation and reduced heart rate and contractility. They are used in black and elderly patients; labetalol in hypertension with pregnancy and IV for hypertensive emergencies; carvedilol to treat heart failure. Their main side effects are orthostatic hypotension and dizziness. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Labetalol is used in pregnancy and IV for hypertensive emergencies, not named for heart failure.
x.2: Prazosin is a selective alpha-1 blocker.
x.3: Esmolol is on the sympathoplegic list but is not an alpha-beta blocker.

m.1: mixes up labetalol and carvedilol uses

items.q: A nurse reviews the vasodilators used in hypertension. Match each drug to its mechanism of action.

choices: Production of nitric oxide in arterioles and veins
Uncertain; perhaps inhibition of Ca++ release and NO release

items.w: The direct vasodilators differ by site and mechanism. Nitroprusside acts on arterioles and veins by producing nitric oxide. Minoxidil and diazoxide open K+ channels in arterioles. Fenoldopam activates D1 receptors in arterioles. Hydralazine relaxes arterioles by an uncertain mechanism, perhaps inhibiting Ca++ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and stimulating NO release. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.4: Alpha-1 blockade is the mechanism of prazosin, not a direct vasodilator.

m.4: mixes up alpha blockers and direct vasodilators

items.q: A client has received a nitroprusside infusion for several days. Which toxicity should the nurse monitor for?
items.w: Nitroprusside is rapidly metabolized by red blood cells, liberating cyanide, which is then metabolized to thiocyanate. Its half-life is about 2 minutes, so it must be given by continuous infusion. Adverse effects include excessive vasodilation, rebound hypertension, palpitations, nausea, substernal pain and cyanide toxicity. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Lupoid syndrome is an immunological adverse effect of hydralazine.
x.2: Hypertrichosis is an adverse effect of minoxidil.
x.3: Hyperglycemia is an adverse effect of diazoxide.

m.1: mixes up nitroprusside and hydralazine toxicity

items.q: A nurse states that nitroprusside has a half-life of about 2 minutes and must be given by continuous infusion.
items.w: True. Nitroprusside's half-life is about 2 minutes, so it must be given by continuous infusion to be effective. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: This statement is true: half-life about 2 minutes, continuous infusion.

items.q: A client takes high-dose hydralazine. Which adverse effect is immunological rather than an extension of the drug's vasodilator action?
items.w: Hydralazine relaxes small arteries and arterioles. Headache, dizziness, palpitations and flushing extend that vasodilator effect. Separately, immunological reactions occur: lupoid syndrome (up to 20% with very high doses), fever, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia and vasculitis. It is used with isosorbide mononitrate in heart failure. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: Headache is an extension of the pharmacological (vasodilator) effect.
x.2: Palpitations are an extension of the pharmacological effect.
x.3: Flushing is an extension of the pharmacological effect.

items.q: A client on minoxidil for severe hypertension notices increased hair growth on the face and arms. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: It is hypertrichosis, a known adverse effect of minoxidil.
It is a sign of cyanide toxicity.
It is part of a lupoid syndrome.
It means the drug is acting as a diuretic.
items.w: Minoxidil is a prodrug that the liver converts to an active K+ channel opener in arterioles. Because of its toxicity it is reserved for severe hypertension that responds poorly to other drugs. Adverse effects are salt and water retention, tachycardia, palpitations, flushing and hypertrichosis, which is why it is also used locally to treat baldness. (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.2: Lupoid syndrome is a hydralazine adverse effect.
x.3: Minoxidil causes salt and water retention, not diuresis.

items.q: A client with diabetes receives diazoxide for a hypertensive emergency. Which value should the nurse monitor closely?
o: Blood glucose, because diazoxide causes hyperglycemia
Urine output, because diazoxide causes strong diuresis
Blood cyanide, because diazoxide releases cyanide
Coombs' test, because diazoxide causes hemolysis

x.1: Diazoxide does NOT cause diuresis (it lacks a sulfonamide group); it causes salt and water retention.

x.3: A positive Coombs' test is caused by methyldopa.

items.q: Fenoldopam is ordered for several clients with severe hypertension. For which client should the nurse question the order?

A client who needs renal vasodilation
items.w: Fenoldopam, the only D1-receptor agonist, is given by IV infusion for hypertensive emergencies. It dilates mainly renal and mesenteric vessels and increases natriuresis. Its adverse effects explain its contraindications: reflex tachycardia (angina), a dose-dependent rise in intraocular pressure (glaucoma) and a fall in serum potassium (hypokalemic states). (Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension))

x.1: A hypertensive emergency is fenoldopam's therapeutic use.

items.q: A client replaces butter with olive oil in cooking. Which change in blood lipids should the nurse expect?

Lower total and LDL-cholesterol with lower HDL-cholesterol
Lower triacylglycerol with little effect on LDL or HDL

items.q: A nurse explains fatty acid naming to a client. In an omega-3 fat, the first double bond begins at carbon number ____ counting from the methyl end.
