items.q: A nurse teaches a client how to spot trans fats when shopping. Which words on an ingredient list indicate trans fatty acids?
items.w: Trans fatty acids are not found in plants and occur only in small amounts in animal foods, but they are formed during hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils, as in margarine manufacture. The key to their presence in a food is the words "partially hydrogenated" on the ingredient list. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD), slide note (key to trans fats))

x.1: Olive oil is a monounsaturated fat, not a trans fat.
x.2: Plant sterols lower LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption.
x.3: Fish oils are omega-3 fats.

m.2: confuses plant sterols with trans fats

items.q: A nurse explains that trans fatty acids are chemically unsaturated but behave more like saturated fatty acids.
items.w: True. Trans fatty acids are chemically classified as unsaturated, but they behave more like saturated fatty acids: they raise LDL-cholesterol, lower HDL-cholesterol and increase CHD risk. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: This statement is true: trans fats are unsaturated yet act like saturated fats.

items.q: A nurse states that WHO recommends limiting trans fat to less than 10% of total energy intake.
items.w: False. WHO recommends limiting trans fat to less than 1% of total energy intake, which is less than 2.2 g per day on a 2000-calorie diet. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.0: The WHO limit is less than 1% of energy (under 2.2 g/day on 2000 kcal).

items.q: A nurse reviews dietary fats with a client. Match each type of fat to its effect on blood lipids.

choices: Lowers triacylglycerol with little effect on LDL or HDL

items.w: Each fat has a signature effect. Saturated fats raise total and LDL-cholesterol. Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL. Monounsaturated fats lower LDL and raise HDL. Omega-6 fats lower both LDL and HDL. Omega-3 fats lower triacylglycerol, suppress arrhythmia, thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL or HDL. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.4: Lowering both LDL and HDL is the effect of omega-6 fats.

m.4: mixes up omega-3 and omega-6 effects

rs.0: A client eats a diet high in saturated fat. Which effect on blood lipids should the nurse expect?
rs.1: A client eats many foods made with partially hydrogenated oil. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?
rs.2: A client substitutes monounsaturated fat for saturated fat. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?
rs.3: A client adds fish oil (omega-3) to the diet. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?

items.q: A nurse teaches a client about diet and cholesterol. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "The cholesterol I eat affects my blood cholesterol more than the type of fat I eat."
"Cholesterol is found only in animal products."
"Plant sterols lower LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption in my gut."
items.w: Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products, but its effect on blood cholesterol is LESS important than the amount and type of fatty acids eaten. A client who believes the opposite needs more teaching. Plant sterols in fortified margarines reduce LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption, and fish oils reduce triacylglycerol. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: This is accurate: dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products, so no teaching is needed.
x.2: This is accurate: plant sterols inhibit intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
x.3: This is accurate: omega-3 fish oils reduce blood triacylglycerol.

items.q: A client with high cholesterol asks which dietary factors help lower blood cholesterol. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Antioxidants such as vitamins E and C
items.w: The dietary factors listed as decreasing blood cholesterol are omega-6 polyunsaturated fats, monounsaturated fats, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber and large doses of vitamin B3. Saturated and trans fats push cholesterol the other way. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.5: Saturated fats RAISE total and LDL-cholesterol.
x.6: Partially hydrogenated oils contain trans fats, which raise LDL.

m.5: thinks saturated fat lowers cholesterol
m.6: thinks margarine trans fats are protective

items.q: A nurse explains oxidative stress to a client with coronary disease. Which definition is accurate?
o: An imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants that can lead to damage
Any production of reactive oxygen species in the body
An excess of antioxidants over oxidants
The buildup of lipid-rich plaque in the intima
items.w: Oxidative stress is a state in which reactive species increase without a matching increase in antioxidants: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage. Reactive oxygen species are not always harmful; phagocytes use them to kill microbes. The imbalance is what has been implicated in diseases such as atherosclerosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: ROS are made normally and can be useful (e.g. microbial killing); stress is the IMBALANCE.
x.2: That is the opposite of oxidative stress.
x.3: That describes atherosclerosis, which oxidative stress helps cause.

m.1: thinks any ROS is oxidative stress
m.2: reverses the imbalance

items.q: A nurse reviews reactive nitrogen species. Which one is a NON-radical?
items.w: Reactive species are split into radicals, which carry an unpaired electron, and non-radicals, which are strong oxidants or favor strong oxidant formation. Among reactive nitrogen species, nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide are radicals and peroxynitrite is a non-radical. Among reactive oxygen species, superoxide, hydroxyl and peroxyl are radicals; hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid and ozone are not. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: Nitric oxide (NO.) is a free radical.
x.2: Nitrogen dioxide (NO2.) is a free radical.
x.3: Superoxide is a reactive OXYGEN species and a radical.

m.1: thinks NO is a non-radical

items.q: A nurse states that hydrogen peroxide is a free radical because it has an unpaired electron.
items.w: False. Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a NON-radical reactive oxygen species: a strong oxidant without an unpaired electron. The ROS radicals are superoxide, hydroxyl and peroxyl. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.0: H2O2 is a non-radical ROS.

items.q: A nurse reviews ENDOGENOUS sources of free radicals in a client's cells. Which sources apply? Select all that apply.
o: Leakage of electrons from the respiratory chain
items.w: Endogenous free radicals come from cellular metabolism: electron leakage from the respiratory chain, oxidase enzymes such as xanthine oxidase, prostaglandin synthesis, production of nitric oxide from arginine and phagocytosis (myeloperoxidase, NADPH oxidase). Exogenous sources are drug metabolism, ionizing radiation and cigarette smoke. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.4: Cigarette smoke is an exogenous (environmental) source.
x.5: Ionizing radiation is an exogenous source.
x.6: Drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450) is listed as exogenous.

m.4: mixes up endogenous and exogenous sources
m.5: mixes up endogenous and exogenous sources

items.q: A client's neutrophils engulf bacteria. Arrange the steps of the oxygen-dependent killing pathway in order.
o: Bacteria are phagocytosed and ROS production rises (respiratory burst)
NADPH oxidase converts molecular oxygen into superoxide
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide
Myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 and chloride into hypochlorous acid
items.w: Reactive oxygen species are sometimes useful. In neutrophils and monocytes, phagocytosis triggers a rapid rise in ROS called the respiratory burst. NADPH oxidase converts oxygen to superoxide, superoxide dismutase converts it to H2O2, and myeloperoxidase uses H2O2 and chloride ions to make hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria. H2O2 can also form hydroxyl radicals in a reaction catalyzed by free ferrous ions. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

items.q: A client with severe sepsis has very high nitric oxide production driven by bacterial toxins and cytokines. Which enzyme is responsible?
items.w: Nitric oxide is made from L-arginine by NO synthase. eNOS (endothelium) and nNOS (neural) are constitutive and produce low levels constantly. iNOS is expressed in many cells including macrophages and neutrophils; it is induced by bacterial toxins, TNF and inflammatory cytokines and can produce large amounts of NO for hours or days, so it is linked to inflammation. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: eNOS is constitutive and constantly produces LOW levels of NO.
x.2: nNOS is constitutive and produces low levels of NO in neurons.
x.3: Xanthine oxidase is an oxidase that produces ROS, not NO.

m.1: mixes up eNOS and iNOS

items.q: A client with angina takes sublingual nitroglycerin. How does it relieve coronary spasm?
o: It is metabolized into nitric oxide, which causes vasodilation.
It is converted into superoxide, which relaxes smooth muscle.
It acts as an antioxidant that neutralizes oxidized LDL.
items.w: NO produced by endothelial NOS improves vascular dilation and perfusion, which is beneficial. Vasodilators such as nitroglycerin are metabolized into NO and so dilate coronary arteries in spasm in angina, a therapeutic and diagnostic use. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: Superoxide is a damaging ROS radical, not a vasodilator.
x.2: Nitroglycerin works through NO-mediated vasodilation, not as an antioxidant.
x.3: iNOS induction is linked to inflammation, not to nitroglycerin's therapeutic effect.

m.3: mixes up iNOS and therapeutic NO

items.q: A nurse explains that nitric oxide is a free-radical gas with a half-life of seconds that is made from L-arginine.
items.w: True. NO is a free radical gas with a very short half-life (seconds), synthesized by NO synthase from L-arginine and metabolized into nitrates, nitrites and peroxynitrite. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: This statement is true: NO is a short-lived radical made from L-arginine.

items.q: A nurse reviews the body's antioxidant defenses with a client. Match each antioxidant to its type.
items.w: Antioxidants are enzymatic (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase with glutathione reductase and G6PD) or non-enzymatic. Non-enzymatic antioxidants are nutrient (carotene, tocopherol, ascorbic acid, selenium) or metabolic (glutathione, thioredoxin, ceruloplasmin, albumin, melatonin, transferrin, ferritin, uric acid). (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.3: Transition metals favor the formation of strong oxidants; they are not antioxidants.

m.3: thinks metals are antioxidants

rs.0: A nurse explains how superoxide dismutase protects cells. What type of antioxidant is it?
rs.1: A client takes vitamin E supplements. What type of antioxidant is vitamin E?
rs.2: A nurse describes glutathione to a client. What type of antioxidant is it?
rs.3: A nurse reviews catalase. What type of antioxidant is it?

items.q: A nurse explains how oxidized LDL drives atherosclerosis. Arrange the key stages in order.
o: Endothelial dysfunction from hypertension, smoking or dyslipidemia
LDL enters the intima and is oxidized
Adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1) and MCP-1 recruit monocytes
Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL and become foam cells (fatty streak)
Smooth muscle cells migrate and form a fibrous cap
Plaque rupture or erosion triggers thrombosis
items.w: Stressors damage the endothelium. LDL passes into the intima and is oxidized by free radicals and lipoxygenases. Activated endothelium expresses VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and MCP-1 that recruit monocytes and T cells. Monocytes become macrophages that engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors and become foam cells, forming the fatty streak. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, proliferate and lay down a fibrous cap; a necrotic core and calcification follow, and a vulnerable plaque may rupture and trigger thrombosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress), key stages slide)

items.q: A nurse explains how fatty streaks form in a client's arteries. How do macrophages take up oxidized LDL?
o: Through scavenger receptors, turning into lipid-laden foam cells
Through VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 on the macrophage
By efferocytosis of dead smooth muscle cells
By secreting collagen around the lipid
items.w: Monocytes recruited into the intima differentiate into macrophages and engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors, becoming lipid-laden foam cells. The initial accumulation of foam cells creates the earliest visible lesion, the fatty streak. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 are adhesion molecules on activated ENDOTHELIAL cells that capture monocytes.
x.2: Efferocytosis is clearing dead cells; its failure enlarges the necrotic core.
x.3: Collagen and proteoglycans are made by smooth muscle cells forming the fibrous cap.

m.1: mixes up adhesion molecules and scavenger receptors

items.q: A nurse reviews why some atherosclerotic plaques develop a large necrotic core. Which process is responsible?
o: Apoptosis of macrophages and SMCs with impaired clearance of the dead cells (efferocytosis)
Migration of smooth muscle cells to form a fibrous cap
Expression of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 by endothelial cells
items.w: As plaques progress, macrophages and smooth muscle cells undergo apoptosis and secondary necrosis. When the dead cells are not cleared (impaired efferocytosis), an acellular necrotic core rich in lipids and debris enlarges, and calcium salts deposit, causing calcification. Vulnerable plaques can then rupture or erode and trigger thrombosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: SMC migration builds the fibrous cap over the lipid core, not the necrotic core.
x.2: Adhesion molecules recruit monocytes early in the process.
x.3: Blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption is how plant sterols lower LDL.

m.1: mixes up cap formation and necrotic core

items.q: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath for 2 weeks. He reports painful nodules on his fingertips and a new heart murmur. His past medical history is significant for intravenous drug use. Temperature 38.9°C, HR 110 bpm, BP 110/65 mmHg, RR 20/min; WBC 15,000/µL, ESR elevated; 3 sets of blood cultures show Gram-positive cocci in clusters; echocardiography shows vegetations on the tricuspid valve. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.w: Intravenous drug use endocarditis mainly affects the tricuspid valve, and Staphylococcus aureus is its main cause and the most common cause of IE overall. S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive, and causes an acute, aggressive infection with rapid valve destruction. Painful finger-pad nodules are Osler nodes. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis), in-class case)

x.1: Viridans streptococci are Gram-positive cocci in CHAINS that cause subacute IE on damaged valves, often after oral sources.
x.2: Enterococcus faecalis causes IE in the elderly after GU or GI procedures; it does not grow in clusters.
x.3: Haemophilus is a HACEK Gram-negative bacillus, not a Gram-positive coccus.

m.1: picks viridans for any endocarditis

items.q: A client with known rheumatic valve disease has had low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss for 6 weeks after a dental extraction. Which organism should the nurse suspect?
items.w: Subacute IE progresses slowly over weeks to months, usually in people with preexisting valve disease such as rheumatic heart disease, and causes milder symptoms such as low-grade fever, malaise, chills and weight loss. It is caused by less virulent organisms: viridans streptococci (notably S. mutans) from the oral cavity, enterococci and the HACEK group. A dental procedure is a classic source of the transient bacteremia. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: S. aureus causes ACUTE, rapidly progressive IE, often on healthy valves.
x.2: S. epidermidis is typical of prosthetic valve and device infections.
x.3: S. bovis is associated with colorectal carcinoma or GI lesions, not dental sources.

m.1: mixes up acute and subacute organisms

items.q: A client who had a prosthetic valve inserted 3 months ago develops endocarditis. Which organism is most likely?
items.w: Prosthetic valve endocarditis is early when it develops within 12 months of surgery, often from intraoperative contamination, and late after 12 months from community-acquired infection. It is caused mostly by Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus; S. epidermidis is closely associated with indwelling devices and catheters. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: Viridans streptococci cause subacute IE on damaged native valves after oral sources.
x.2: S. bovis is linked to colorectal carcinoma and GI lesions.
x.3: S. pneumoniae is a rare cause of IE.

m.1: picks viridans for any endocarditis

items.q: A nurse states that endocarditis in clients who inject drugs mainly affects the tricuspid valve.
items.w: True. Intravenous drug abuse endocarditis mainly affects the tricuspid valve and is caused mostly by S. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Candida. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: This statement is true: IVDU endocarditis is mainly tricuspid.

items.q: A nurse states that subacute infective endocarditis usually affects healthy valves and is mostly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
items.w: False. That describes ACUTE IE. Subacute IE usually occurs on preexisting diseased valves, progresses over weeks to months and is caused by less virulent organisms such as viridans streptococci, enterococci and HACEK. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.0: That is acute IE; subacute IE affects diseased valves with less virulent organisms.

m.0: mixes up acute and subacute IE

items.q: A client's blood cultures grow Streptococcus bovis and echocardiography confirms endocarditis. Which follow-up evaluation should the nurse anticipate?
o: Evaluation for colorectal carcinoma or another GI lesion
A dental examination for an oral source
A review of recent genitourinary procedures
Inspection of a pacemaker pocket for skin contamination
items.w: Streptococcus bovis endocarditis is associated with colorectal carcinoma or other gastrointestinal lesions, so finding it should prompt a search of the bowel. Viridans streptococci point to the mouth, enterococci to GU or GI procedures and staphylococci to skin and devices. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: An oral source is typical of viridans streptococci.
x.2: GU and GI procedures are linked with Enterococcus faecalis.
x.3: Skin contamination at implantation causes cardiac device IE, usually staphylococcal.

m.1: links S. bovis to the mouth

items.q: An 80-year-old client develops endocarditis two weeks after a urinary tract procedure in the hospital. Which organism should the nurse suspect?
items.w: Enterococcus faecalis is common in elderly and hospital-acquired IE and is often associated with genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures. It adheres to the damaged valve using teichoic acid. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: S. mutans (viridans group) comes from the oral cavity.
x.2: S. epidermidis is linked to prosthetic valves and indwelling devices.
x.3: Kingella belongs to the HACEK group of pharyngeal flora.

m.1: picks viridans for any endocarditis

items.q: A client has culture-negative endocarditis and HACEK organisms are suspected. Which organisms belong to the HACEK group? Select all that apply.
items.w: HACEK stands for Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella. They are slow-growing, fastidious Gram-negative bacilli of the pharyngeal flora that cause subacute IE with negative blood cultures unless special media are used. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.5: Klebsiella is a rare Gram-negative cause of IE, mainly in immunocompromised clients, not a HACEK member.
x.6: Enterococcus faecalis is a Gram-positive coccus, not a HACEK member.
x.7: E. coli is a rare Gram-negative cause, not a HACEK member.

m.5: thinks the K in HACEK is Klebsiella
m.6: thinks the E in HACEK is Enterococcus
m.7: thinks the E in HACEK is E. coli

items.q: A nurse explains to a client with valve disease how endocarditis develops. Arrange the steps in order.
o: Platelets and fibrin form a sterile microthrombus
Transient bacteremia, e.g. after a dental procedure
Circulating microbes adhere to the fibrin-platelet matrix
Bacteria proliferate to form a friable vegetation
Fragments break off as septic emboli
items.w: IE needs endothelial injury, bacteremia and microbial adherence. Damaged valvular endothelium attracts platelets and fibrin, forming a sterile microthrombus. A transient bacteremia from dental procedures, oral or skin infections, IV drug use or invasive procedures seeds the blood, and organisms adhere to the fibrin-platelet matrix. They proliferate inside it to form a vegetation of fibrin, platelets, bacteria and inflammatory cells, which is friable and can fragment into septic emboli. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

items.q: A nurse reviews how organisms stick to damaged heart valves. Match each organism to its adherence factor.

choices: M protein cross-reacting with heart antigens

items.w: After a bacteremia, organisms must adhere to the fibrin-platelet matrix on the valve. S. aureus uses clumping factor and fibronectin-binding protein (protein F), viridans streptococci use dextran, a sticky polysaccharide, Enterococcus faecalis uses teichoic acid, and Gram-negative bacteria use pili. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.4: M-protein cross-reaction is the immune mechanism of rheumatic fever, not a valve adherence factor.

m.4: confuses rheumatic fever with endocarditis

rs.0: A client has S. aureus endocarditis. Which adherence factor lets this organism stick to the valve?
rs.1: A client develops viridans streptococcal endocarditis after dental work. Which adherence factor does the organism use?
rs.2: A client has Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. Which adherence factor does this organism use?
rs.3: A client has Gram-negative bacterial endocarditis. Which structure helps the bacteria adhere?

items.q: A nurse assesses a client with suspected infective endocarditis. Which extracardiac findings are consistent with the diagnosis? Select all that apply.
o: Painless erythematous lesions on the palms and soles
Painful nodules on the pads of the fingers
Firm painless subcutaneous nodules on extensor surfaces
items.w: Septic emboli and immune-mediated injury give IE its extracardiac signs: petechiae, especially splinter hemorrhages under the nails; Janeway lesions (small, nontender, erythematous lesions on palms and soles); Osler nodes (painful nodules on finger and toe pads); and Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages). Rheumatic fever has different skin signs. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.4: Erythema marginatum is a major Jones criterion of acute rheumatic fever.
x.5: Subcutaneous nodules on extensor surfaces belong to acute rheumatic fever.
x.6: Sydenham chorea is a neurologic manifestation of acute rheumatic fever.

m.4: confuses rheumatic fever with endocarditis
m.5: confuses rheumatic fever with endocarditis

items.q: A nurse documents the skin and eye findings of a client with endocarditis. Match each finding to its description.

choices: Small, nontender, erythematous lesions on palms and soles
Painful nodules on the pads of the fingers and toes
Firm painless nodules on extensor surfaces

items.w: The four classic extracardiac signs of IE are easy to mix up. Janeway lesions are nontender and on palms and soles; Osler nodes are painful and on finger and toe pads ("O for ouch"); Roth spots are in the retina; splinter hemorrhages are under the nails. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.4: These are the subcutaneous nodules of acute rheumatic fever.

m.4: confuses rheumatic fever with endocarditis

rs.0: A client with endocarditis has Janeway lesions. Which description should the nurse document?
rs.1: A client with endocarditis has Osler nodes. Which description fits?
rs.2: A client with endocarditis has Roth spots on eye examination. What are they?
rs.3: A nurse notes splinter hemorrhages in a client with endocarditis. Where are they found?

items.q: A client is admitted with suspected infective endocarditis and empiric antibiotics are ordered. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Draw three sets of blood cultures from different venipuncture sites before the first antibiotic dose.
Give the first antibiotic dose, then draw blood cultures.
Draw one set of blood cultures from the existing IV line.
Wait for the echocardiogram before drawing any cultures.
items.w: Blood cultures are the gold standard for diagnosing IE: three sets from different venipuncture sites, taken before treatment. Empiric antibiotics start once cultures have been sampled, then switch to targeted therapy when results are available. Giving antibiotics first is a leading cause of culture-negative endocarditis. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis), slide note (gold standard))

x.1: Prior antibiotic therapy is a main cause of culture-negative endocarditis.
x.2: The standard is three sets from different venipuncture sites.
x.3: Blood cultures are the gold standard and are taken before treatment; empiric therapy starts once they are sampled.

m.1: gives antibiotics before cultures

items.q: A client's blood cultures stay negative despite clinical endocarditis. Which causes should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Antibiotics given before the cultures were drawn
A fastidious organism such as Coxiella burnetii or Bartonella
Drawing three sets from different venipuncture sites
items.w: Culture-negative endocarditis has three main causes: prior antibiotic therapy before cultures, fastidious bacteria (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella and the HACEK group), which are confirmed by serology or PCR, and fungal infection. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.4: S. aureus grows readily; it is the classic culture-positive cause.
x.5: Three sets from different sites is the correct technique, not a cause of negative cultures.

m.4: thinks S. aureus is hard to culture

items.q: A client with a native valve has suspected endocarditis and blood cultures have been drawn. Which empiric regimen should the nurse anticipate?
o: Vancomycin plus cefepime plus gentamicin plus rifampin
items.w: Empiric therapy starts once blood cultures have been sampled. Native valve endocarditis: vancomycin plus cefepime. Prosthetic valve endocarditis: vancomycin plus cefepime plus gentamicin plus rifampin. Therapy is switched to targeted antibiotics when culture results arrive, and antithrombotic agents are part of treatment. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: This four-drug regimen is for PROSTHETIC valve endocarditis.
x.2: Amoxicillin is a prophylaxis regimen before dental or invasive procedures.
x.3: Azithromycin is a prophylaxis option for penicillin-allergic clients.

m.1: mixes up native and prosthetic valve regimens
m.2: confuses prophylaxis with treatment

items.q: A client with a prosthetic heart valve and a penicillin allergy is scheduled for a dental extraction. Which prophylaxis should the nurse anticipate?
o: Vancomycin plus cefepime for several weeks
No prophylaxis, because dental procedures are low risk
items.w: Endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated before dental or invasive procedures in clients with high-risk cardiac features or a prosthetic valve, given 30-60 minutes before. Without penicillin allergy, amoxicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin is used; with penicillin allergy, a macrolide such as azithromycin or doxycycline. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.1: Amoxicillin is a penicillin; it is the choice only without penicillin allergy.
x.2: This is empiric TREATMENT of native valve endocarditis, not prophylaxis.
x.3: Prophylaxis is indicated before dental procedures in clients with a prosthetic valve.

m.1: ignores the penicillin allergy
m.2: confuses prophylaxis with treatment

items.q: A nurse reviews laboratory reports from clients with endocarditis. Match each organism to its identifying result.

choices: Cocci in clusters, catalase positive, coagulase negative
Cocci in chains, alpha hemolysis, optochin resistant
Lancet-shaped diplococci, optochin sensitive, bile soluble
Cocci in chains, beta hemolysis, catalase negative

items.w: Staphylococci grow in clusters and are catalase positive; coagulase separates S. aureus (positive, golden colonies, beta hemolysis, mannitol fermenter) from S. epidermidis (negative). Streptococci grow in chains: viridans streptococci are alpha hemolytic, optochin resistant and bile insoluble, S. pneumoniae is alpha hemolytic but optochin sensitive and bile soluble, and S. pyogenes is beta hemolytic and catalase negative. (Microbiology L3 slides (infective endocarditis))

x.4: This is Streptococcus pyogenes.

m.4: mixes up streptococcal hemolysis patterns

rs.0: A client's blood culture grows S. aureus. Which laboratory result identifies it?
rs.1: A client with a prosthetic valve grows S. epidermidis. Which laboratory result identifies it?
rs.2: A client's blood culture grows viridans streptococci. Which laboratory result identifies them?
rs.3: A client's culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Which laboratory result identifies it?

items.q: A nurse reviews the embryology of a child's head arteries. Which artery develops from the remaining part of the 1st aortic arch?
items.w: The first two arch vessels largely disappear. The remaining part of the 1st arch forms the maxillary arteries and the remaining part of the 2nd arch forms the stapedial arteries. The 3rd arch gives the carotids, the 4th the aortic arch and right subclavian, and the 6th the pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus. (Embryology L3 slides (aortic arches))

x.1: The stapedial artery is the remnant of the 2nd arch.
x.2: The common carotid comes from the proximal part of the 3rd arch.
x.3: The external carotid is a new bud from the junction of the common and internal carotids.

m.1: mixes up the 1st and 2nd arches

items.q: A nurse reviews which adult vessels come from each aortic arch. Match each arch to its derivative.

choices: Arch of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian
Proximal part of the right subclavian artery

items.w: The 3rd arches form the common carotids (proximal parts) and, with the dorsal aorta, the internal carotids. The left 4th arch forms the part of the aortic arch between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, and the right 4th arch forms the proximal right subclavian. The 5th arch disappears. The left 6th arch forms the left pulmonary artery (proximal) and the ductus arteriosus (distal). (Embryology L3 slides (aortic arches))

x.4: The 5th arch vessel disappears completely.

m.4: thinks the 5th arch persists

rs.0: A nurse reviews the 3rd aortic arch. What do its proximal parts form?
rs.1: A child has an anomaly of the left 4th aortic arch. Which adult vessel segment develops from it?
rs.2: A nurse explains the right 4th aortic arch. Which adult vessel does it form?
rs.3: A newborn has a patent vessel formed from the distal left 6th arch. Which vessel is it?

items.q: A student nurse asks what happens to the 5th aortic arch vessel. Which response is accurate?
o: It forms the right pulmonary artery.
items.w: Of the six pairs of aortic arch vessels, the 1st and 2nd leave small remnants (maxillary and stapedial arteries), the 3rd, 4th and 6th form major vessels, and the 5th disappears completely. (Embryology L3 slides (aortic arches))

x.1: The stapedial artery comes from the 2nd arch.

anat-coronary.title: Coronary arteries: origin, course and territories
points: Right coronary artery: from the right (anterior) aortic sinus; left coronary artery: from the left (anterior) aortic sinus.

The posterior interventricular artery (PDA) runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the diaphragmatic surface of both ventricles and the posterior 1/3 of the septum.
Artery to the SA node: RCA 65%, circumflex 35%. Artery to the AV node: RCA 80%, circumflex 20%.

anat-carotid.title: Common, external and internal carotid arteries
points: Right common carotid: from the brachiocephalic artery behind the sternoclavicular joint; left common carotid: from the arch of the aorta.
The common carotid ascends in the carotid sheath, related medially to the trachea and larynx and laterally to the IJV, and ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-4).
The external carotid ends in the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

The internal carotid has no branches in the neck; it enters the skull through the carotid canal.

phys-av-block.title: AV nodal blocks
points: 1st degree: PR interval > 0.20 s; prolonged conduction delay in the AV node or bundle of His.
2nd degree Mobitz I: PR progressively lengthens until one impulse (usually the 3rd or 4th) fails to make it through the AV node.

3rd degree: complete block in the AV junction; atria and ventricles beat independently; ventricular pacemaker at 30-45 beats/minute.
When an impulse originates in a ventricle, conduction is inefficient and the QRS is wide and bizarre.

phys-co.title: Cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction
points: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 = 4900 ml/min, about 5 L/min.
Stroke volume = EDV - ESV (about 70-80 ml); EDV about 120-130 ml; ESV about 50-60 ml.
EF = SV / EDV x 100; normal 50-75%, up to 90% in strenuous exercise; 30% or less in a failing heart.
Cardiac index = cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area; normal 3.2 L/min/m2.
Cardiac reserve = the difference between cardiac output at rest and the maximum the heart can pump per minute.

phys-autonomic.title: Autonomic control of heart rate and contractility
points: Parasympathetic (vagus) mainly supplies the atria (SA and AV nodes); parasympathetic innervation of the ventricles is sparse.
Parasympathetic: decreases heart rate, increases AV nodal delay, decreases atrial contractility, no effect on ventricular muscle.
Sympathetic: increases heart rate, decreases AV nodal delay, hastens ventricular conduction, increases atrial and ventricular contractility, promotes adrenal epinephrine.
Under resting conditions parasympathetic discharge dominates.

phys-starling.title: Frank-Starling law, preload and afterload
points: Frank-Starling law: force of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber (EDV and stroke volume).
Resting cardiac fiber length is less than optimum, so more filling stretches fibers closer to optimum and increases the force of the next contraction.
Preload = load before contraction, the end-diastolic volume. Afterload = load the ventricle pumps against, the arterial blood pressure.
Sympathetic stimulation and epinephrine increase contractility at any EDV (more Ca2+ influx) and shift the Frank-Starling curve to the left.

phys-venous-return.title: Factors controlling venous return
points: Veins are capacitance vessels holding about 60-70% of blood; when veins store less blood, more returns to the heart.
Skeletal muscle pump: contraction compresses veins and moves blood toward the heart.
Respiratory pump: in inspiration intrathoracic pressure falls (-5 mmHg), drawing blood into the chest.
Sympathetic venoconstriction, the cardiac suction effect and one-way venous valves (every 2-4 cm) also increase venous return.

phys-co-measure.title: Measuring cardiac output and conditions that change it
points: Fick principle: cardiac output = O2 uptake by the lungs / (arterial O2 - venous O2), e.g. 200 / (200 - 160) = 5 L/min.
Cardiac output rises in hyperthyroidism, anemia and fever; falls in hypothyroidism, myocardial damage and failure, valvular disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage and shock.
Most common causes of heart failure: myocardial infarction, then working against increased afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis).

phys-coronary-flow.title: Coronary blood flow and oxygen extraction
points: Coronary blood flow at rest is about 225-250 ml/minute, about 5% of cardiac output.
At rest the heart extracts 60-70% of the oxygen from each unit of blood (other tissues about 25%).
Up to 40% of the cardiac cell is mitochondria, so the heart needs more O2; when more O2 is needed, delivery rises only by increasing blood flow.
The heart uses mainly free fatty acids; in ischemia it uses anaerobic glycolysis, forming lactic acid (one cause of cardiac pain).

phys-phasic-flow.title: Phasic changes in coronary flow
points: Left ventricular flow falls in systole: the contracting LV compresses the coronary arteries and the open aortic valve partially blocks their entrance.
Systole: aorta 120, LV 121 mmHg (gradient -1); diastole: aorta 80, LV 0 (gradient 80). Right ventricle gradient is 95 in systole, 80 in diastole.
The subendocardial surface of the left ventricle gets almost no flow in systole, so it is the most common site of myocardial infarction.
Tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces coronary flow; aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure also reduce LV flow.

phys-coronary-control.title: Chemical and neural control of coronary flow
points: Coronary blood flow shows considerable autoregulation.
Vasodilators: lack of oxygen, increased CO2, H+, K+, lactate, prostaglandins, adenosine and adenine nucleotides.
Adenosine, formed from ATP during cardiac metabolic activity, causes coronary vasodilatation.

Direct sympathetic effect: alpha-receptor vasoconstriction (seen when beta receptors are blocked). Indirect effect in the intact body: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, releasing vasodilator metabolites.
Parasympathetic influences are minor and weakly vasodilatory.

phys-ihd.title: Ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction
points: Risk factors of IHD: cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, increased lipids (cholesterol), lack of exercise, anxiety.
Angina: retrosternal tightness or pain for a few minutes, often radiating to the inner side of the left arm, precipitated by effort and relieved by rest.
MI: at least 75% of the coronary lumen blocked by thrombus.
ECG: ST depression in IHD; ST elevation in MI, in the respective leads.
Treatment: coronary dilators (nitrates), beta-blockers, angioplasty, stent, bypass surgery.

path-congestion.title: Hyperemia and congestion
points: Hyperemia: an active process in which arteriolar dilation increases blood flow; tissue turns red (erythema) from oxygenated blood.
Congestion: a passive process from impaired venous outflow; tissue is dusky reddish-blue (cyanosis) from deoxygenated blood.
Acute localized congestion: sudden complete venous obstruction (DVT, ligature, twisted pedicle of an ovary) causing rapid edema and hemorrhage.
Chronic generalized venous congestion is caused by chronic right-sided heart failure; acute generalized congestion by acute heart failure.

path-edema.title: Edema: causes and classification
points: Edema: an abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues; fluid may be transudate, exudate or lymph.
Causes: increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction.
Hypoproteinemia: total plasma proteins below 2.5 gm% or serum albumin below 1.5 gm%.
Pitting edema: generalized edema and obstructive venous edema. Non-pitting: inflammatory and lymphatic edema.

path-ischemia-infarct.title: Ischemia and infarction
points: Ischemia: deficient arterial blood supply due to partial or complete occlusion of the artery; acute (sudden complete) or chronic (gradual partial).
Organs with good collateral circulation show no effect; poor collateral circulation leads to infarction (acute) or chronic ischemic changes.
Infarct: an area of ischemic necrosis from occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage; 99% from thrombosis or embolism.
Red infarct: venous occlusion (ovary), loose tissue (lung), dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine), reperfusion after angioplasty.
White infarct: arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (heart, spleen, kidney); tissue density limits seepage of blood.

path-virchow.title: Thrombosis and Virchow's triad
points: Thrombosis: formation of a compact mass of circulating blood elements inside the cardiovascular system during life.
Virchow's triad: endothelial injury/dysfunction, alterations in blood flow (stasis or turbulence), hypercoagulability.
Endothelial dysfunction increases procoagulants (thromboplastin, vWF, PAI) and decreases anticoagulants (thrombomodulin, antithrombin III, NO, PA).
Stasis reduces inflow of fresh blood containing natural anticoagulants and retards removal of small platelet aggregates.

Acquired hypercoagulability: prolonged bed rest, surgery, burns, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, disseminated cancer, smoking, DIC. Hereditary: factor V and prothrombin gene mutations, antithrombin III deficiency.

path-thrombus-types.title: Sites, types and fate of thrombi
points: Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis, red thrombi) are the most common type, associated with stasis and hypercoagulability.
DVT sites: popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; complication: embolism to the lungs (pulmonary infarction).
Arterial thrombosis is less common because of rapid flow and the thick elastic arterial wall; most common cause is atherosclerosis (coronary, cerebral, femoral).
Cardiac thrombi: auricular thrombus in the left atrium in mitral stenosis; mural thrombus in the left ventricle over an infarct; vegetations on valves.
Fate: dissolution, propagation (a tail liable to detach), embolization, organization and recanalization.

path-embolism.title: Embolism and pulmonary embolism
points: An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a site distant from its origin.
Thromboemboli are the most common type (99%); others: fat, parasitic, air or nitrogen, amniotic fluid, tumor, cholesterol and foreign body emboli.
Pulmonary emboli: 95% originate from deep vein thrombi of the legs; seen in up to 25-30% of DVT patients; 60-80% are small and silent.

Saddle embolus causes sudden death (acute right failure); medium emboli give hemorrhage in a normal lung or infarction in a congested lung; small repeated emboli give pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

path-systemic-emboli.title: Systemic, fat, air and amniotic fluid emboli
points: Systemic emboli: 80% from intracardiac thrombi (2/3 left ventricular wall infarcts, 1/3 dilated left atria or vegetations); also aortic aneurysm, ulcerated plaques, paradoxical emboli.
Paradoxical emboli start as venous emboli but pass through an interatrial or interventricular defect into the systemic circulation.
Site of arrest: 75% lower extremities, 10% brain.
Fat embolism: long bone fracture is the most common cause; the syndrome begins 1-3 days after injury with tachypnea, dyspnea, tachycardia, neurologic symptoms, thrombocytopenia and anemia.
Air embolism needs more than 100 cc of air for a pulmonary effect; causes include neck vein injury, chest wall injury, obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, bypass surgery and decompression sickness.
Amniotic fluid embolism: 1 in 40,000 deliveries, mortality 80%; sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, shock, seizures, pulmonary edema and DIC.

path-arf.title: Acute rheumatic fever: pathogenesis and lesions
points: ARF is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease a few weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
It appears 10 days to 6 weeks after pharyngitis, in about 3% of infected patients, most often in children aged 5-15.
Antibodies and CD4+ T cells against streptococcal M proteins cross-react with self antigens in the heart.
Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic: focal necrosis, T lymphocytes and Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells with a slender wavy ribbon of chromatin.
Pancarditis: fibrinous "bread and butter" pericarditis, myocarditis, and small vegetations along the lines of closure over fibrinoid necrosis (mitral 65%, aortic 25%).

path-jones.title: Jones criteria
points: Major: carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: fever, arthralgia, previous rheumatic fever, raised ESR, CRP or leukocytosis, prolonged PR interval.
Evidence of preceding group A strep: positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or raised or rising streptococcal antibody titer.
Diagnosis: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, supported by evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.
Migratory polyarthritis of large joints is self-limited with no chronic deformities.

path-rhd.title: Chronic rheumatic heart disease and mitral stenosis
points: Endocarditis of ARF heals by fibrosis; repeated pharyngeal infections reactivate the disease and scar the valves.
Mitral valve most commonly affected, then aortic; fibrosis of the leaflets leads to stenosis ("fish mouth" or "buttonhole").
Usually becomes clinically manifest decades after ARF.

Mitral stenosis: left atrial dilatation (with thrombi), chronic pulmonary venous congestion, lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic right-sided failure; the left ventricle is largely unaffected.
Other complications: arrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation), thromboembolism, infective endocarditis.

Atherosclerosis: the most frequent and important pattern.
Mönckeberg medial sclerosis: calcific deposits in muscular arteries in people older than 50.
Arteriolosclerosis: small arteries and arterioles, with hypertension and diabetes; hyaline (amorphous proteinaceous wall) and hyperplastic ("onion-skinning").

path-athero.title: Atherosclerosis: risk factors, pathogenesis and plaque
points: Atherosclerosis: a chronic inflammatory disease of the arterial wall with intimal atheromas that protrude into the lumen and weaken the media.
Non-modifiable risk factors: increasing age, male gender, family history. Modifiable: hyperlipidemia (LDL), hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus.

Response to injury: chronic endothelial injury, endothelial dysfunction with monocyte adhesion, smooth muscle recruitment and macrophage activation, foam cells, then smooth muscle proliferation and collagen deposition.
Fatty spots (<1 mm, foam cells) are the earliest lesion; fatty streaks (1 cm or longer) are not significantly raised and do not disturb blood flow.
Atheroma: raised intimal patch with a soft yellow lipid core under a firm white fibrous cap; cells, ECM and lipid.

Acute plaque changes: rupture, ulceration or erosion (induces thrombosis), and fissure with hemorrhage into the plaque.
Other complications: atheroembolism, aneurysm from weakened media, calcification.
Consequences: ischemic heart disease (coronary), stroke (cerebral), aortic aneurysm (aorta), peripheral vascular disease with gangrene (leg arteries).

pharm-classes.title: Hypertension: definition and drug classes
points: Hypertension is defined as 130/80 mm Hg or higher (ACC/AHA 2023 and Saudi Heart Association).
Classes: diuretics, calcium channel blockers, drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system, sympatholytic drugs, vasodilators.

pharm-diuretics.title: Diuretics in hypertension
points: Early: diuretics lower plasma volume and cardiac output. After 4-8 weeks volume and output return toward normal while peripheral vascular resistance falls (arteriolar vasodilation).
Main mechanism of the vasodilation: depletion of body Na+, lowering smooth muscle Na+ and then intracellular Ca++ via the Na/Ca exchanger.
Thiazides are first choice; antihypertensive doses are lower than diuretic doses.
Loop diuretics are preferable in malignant hypertension and chronic kidney disease.
Potassium-sparing diuretics are used with thiazides to counteract hypokalemia; spironolactone is used in hyperaldosteronism.

pharm-ccb.title: Calcium channel blockers
points: CCBs bind the L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channel from the inner side of the membrane.
Verapamil and diltiazem block Ca++ channels in heart and vessels; dihydropyridines (nifedipine, nicardipine) block vessels only.
Heart rate: increased with dihydropyridines; unchanged or decreased with verapamil and diltiazem. Postural hypotension is negligible.
First-choice drugs, more effective in African patients; nicardipine for hypertensive emergencies; short-acting nifedipine increases mortality.

pharm-ras.title: Renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors and ARBs
points: Aliskiren competitively inhibits renin: angiotensin I, II and aldosterone fall and renin rises; hyperkalemia when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to II and raise bradykinin; less angiotensin II removes negative feedback, so renin rises.
Captopril, lisinopril and enalaprilat are active drugs; enalapril, benazepril and fosinopril are prodrugs activated by the liver; enalaprilat is the IV form.

ACE inhibitor adverse effects: first-dose hypotension, dry cough (bradykinin, prostaglandins or substance P), renal insufficiency in bilateral renal artery stenosis, hyperkalemia, angioedema; pregnancy category D.
ARBs (losartan) selectively block AT1 receptors, inhibit angiotensin more completely and have no effect on bradykinin; contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy.

ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to II and raise bradykinin; less angiotensin II removes negative feedback, so renin rises.
Captopril, lisinopril and enalaprilat are active drugs; enalapril, benazepril and fosinopril are prodrugs activated by the liver; enalaprilat is the IV form.

ACE inhibitor adverse effects: first-dose hypotension, dry cough (bradykinin, prostaglandins or substance P), renal insufficiency in bilateral renal artery stenosis, hyperkalemia, angioedema; pregnancy category D.
ARBs (losartan) selectively block AT1 receptors, inhibit angiotensin more completely and have no effect on bradykinin; contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy.

pharm-central.title: Centrally acting sympatholytics
points: Clonidine and methyldopa are alpha-2 receptor agonists; methyldopa is a false neurotransmitter converted to methylnorepinephrine; clonidine also acts on imidazoline receptors in the medulla.
The final common effect is a decrease in central adrenergic tone.
Second-choice drugs; methyldopa is often preferred in pregnancy.
Adverse effects: sedation, depression, bradycardia, AV block, sexual dysfunction; clonidine withdrawal can cause a hypertensive crisis; methyldopa can cause a positive Coombs' test.

pharm-alpha-beta.title: Alpha blockers, beta blockers and alpha-beta blockers
points: Prazosin and doxazosin selectively block alpha-1 receptors, dilating resistance and capacitance vessels; postural hypotension after the first dose ("first-dose phenomenon").
Beta blockers lower cardiac output (cardiac beta-1) and inhibit renin release (juxtaglomerular beta-1); they do not cause postural hypotension.
Selective beta-1: atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol. Non-selective: propranolol, penbutolol, timolol.
Beta-blocker adverse effects: bradycardia, rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal, bronchoconstriction, insomnia, depression, hypoglycemia, sexual dysfunction.
Labetalol and carvedilol block alpha and beta; labetalol for hypertension in pregnancy and IV in emergencies; carvedilol for heart failure.

pharm-vasodilators.title: Direct vasodilators
points: Nitroprusside: arterioles and veins, nitric oxide; metabolized by red cells releasing cyanide (to thiocyanate); half-life about 2 minutes, continuous infusion; for emergencies, severe heart failure, controlled hypotension.
Hydralazine: arterioles, uncertain mechanism; headache, palpitations, flushing; immunological lupoid syndrome (up to 20% at very high doses).
Minoxidil: arteriolar K+ channel opener, a prodrug; salt and water retention, tachycardia, hypertrichosis; also used for baldness.
Diazoxide: K+ channel opener without diuresis (lacks a sulfonamide group); salt and water retention, hyperglycemia; for hypertensive emergencies.
Fenoldopam: IV D1 agonist, renal and mesenteric vasodilation and natriuresis; reflex tachycardia, raised intraocular pressure, low potassium; contraindicated in angina, glaucoma and hypokalemia.

bio-lipids-chd.title: Blood lipids and coronary heart disease
points: Total blood cholesterol comes from diet and endogenous synthesis and is carried by lipoproteins, especially LDL and HDL.
CHD risk rises with total and LDL cholesterol; high HDL-cholesterol is associated with decreased risk.
Diet control lowers TC and LDL-C by 10-20%; statins lower them by 30-40%.

bio-fats.title: Types of dietary fat and their effects
points: Saturated fats (no double bonds; dairy, meat, coconut and palm oils) raise TC and LDL-C and CHD risk.
Monounsaturated fats (one double bond; olive oil, oleic acid, omega-9) lower TC and LDL-C and raise HDL-C when substituted for saturated fats.
Omega-6 fats (first double bond at carbon 6 from the methyl end; corn, sesame, cottonseed, sunflower oils) lower TC and LDL-C but also lower HDL-C and are proinflammatory.
Omega-3 fats suppress arrhythmia, reduce blood triacylglycerol, decrease thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL-C and HDL-C.
Trans fats are chemically unsaturated but behave like saturated fats: they raise LDL-C and lower HDL-C; formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine).

bio-cholesterol-sterols.title: Dietary cholesterol, plant sterols and cholesterol-lowering factors
points: Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products; its effect on blood cholesterol is less important than the amount and type of fatty acids.
Plant sterols reduce LDL-cholesterol by inhibiting intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
Dietary factors that decrease blood cholesterol: omega-6 PUFA, MUFA, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber, large-dose vitamin B3.

bio-ros.title: Free radicals, ROS and RNS
points: Oxidative stress: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage.
A free radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron in an outer valence shell; it plucks an electron from the nearest molecule.
ROS radicals: superoxide, hydroxyl, peroxyl. ROS non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid, ozone.
RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide. RNS non-radical: peroxynitrite.

Endogenous sources: electron leak from the respiratory chain, oxidases (xanthine oxidase), prostaglandin synthesis, NO from arginine, phagocytosis. Exogenous: drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450), ionizing radiation, cigarette smoke.

bio-burst-no.title: Respiratory burst, nitric oxide and antioxidants
points: Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase converts O2 to superoxide; superoxide dismutase makes H2O2; myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 and chloride to hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria.
NO is a free radical gas with a half-life of seconds, made from L-arginine by NO synthase.
eNOS and nNOS are constitutive and make low levels of NO; iNOS (macrophages, neutrophils; induced by bacterial toxins, TNF, cytokines) makes large amounts for hours or days.
eNOS-derived NO improves vascular dilation and perfusion; nitroglycerin is metabolized to NO and relieves coronary spasm in angina.

Enzymatic antioxidants: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase. Nutrient antioxidants: vitamins A, E, C, selenium. Metabolic: glutathione, ceruloplasmin, albumin, transferrin, ferritin, uric acid.

bio-oxldl.title: Oxidized LDL and the stages of atherosclerosis
points: Free radicals oxidize LDL cholesterol; oxidized LDL triggers inflammation and plaque buildup.

Stages: endothelial dysfunction, LDL retention and oxidation in the intima, recruitment of monocytes and T cells by VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and MCP-1, foam cell formation (fatty streak), SMC migration and fibrous cap, necrotic core and calcification, rupture or erosion with thrombosis.
Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors and become lipid-laden foam cells.
Failure to clear dead macrophages and SMCs (impaired efferocytosis) enlarges an acellular necrotic core.

micro-ie-types.title: Infective endocarditis: classification and organisms
points: IE: infection of the endocardium and its valves (native or prosthetic) with septic vegetations; left-sided in over 95% of cases.
Acute IE: rapid (hours to days), mostly healthy valves, severe symptoms; S. aureus, S. pyogenes; mitral and aortic valves.
Subacute IE: slow (weeks to months), preexisting valve disease, low-grade fever, weight loss; viridans streptococci, enterococci, HACEK.
Prosthetic valve IE: early (within 12 months, intraoperative contamination) or late; mostly S. epidermidis and S. aureus.
IV drug use IE: mainly the tricuspid valve; S. aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Candida.

micro-organisms.title: Specific organisms and their associations
points: S. aureus: most common overall, IV drug users and healthcare-associated IE; acute, rapid valve destruction.
Streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal carcinoma or GI lesions.
Enterococcus faecalis: elderly and hospital-acquired IE, after genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures.

HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, Kingella): slow-growing fastidious Gram-negative bacilli of pharyngeal flora; subacute IE with negative cultures unless special media are used.
Cardiac device IE (pacemaker, ICD) usually comes from skin contamination at implantation; mostly staphylococci.

micro-patho.title: Pathophysiology of infective endocarditis
points: IE needs endothelial injury, bacteremia and microbial adherence leading to vegetation formation.
Damaged valvular endothelium collects platelets and fibrin, forming a sterile microthrombus (sterile vegetation).
Adherence factors: S. aureus clumping factor and fibronectin-binding protein; viridans streptococci dextran; E. faecalis teichoic acid; Gram-negatives pili.
Vegetations contain fibrin, platelets, bacteria and inflammatory cells; they are friable and embolize, and the bacteria are protected from phagocytes and antibiotics.
Consequences: valve destruction with regurgitation and heart failure, septic emboli with infarcts or abscesses, immune complex glomerulonephritis and vasculitis.

micro-signs.title: Clinical features of infective endocarditis
points: Acute: high fever and sepsis. Subacute: mild fever, headache, myalgia, weight loss, night sweats. Cardiac: murmur, heart failure.
Splinter hemorrhages: petechial hemorrhages under the fingernails.
Janeway lesions: small, nontender, erythematous lesions on palms and soles. Osler nodes: painful nodules on the pads of fingers and toes.
Roth spots: retinal hemorrhages.

micro-dx-tx.title: Diagnosis, treatment and prophylaxis
points: Blood cultures are the gold standard: three sets from different venipuncture sites before treatment.
Culture-negative IE: prior antibiotics, fastidious bacteria (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, HACEK; confirm by serology or PCR), fungal infection.
Empiric therapy once cultures are drawn: native valve vancomycin + cefepime; prosthetic valve vancomycin + cefepime + gentamicin + rifampin; then targeted therapy.
Prophylaxis before dental or invasive procedures in high-risk clients, 30-60 minutes before: amoxicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin; if penicillin-allergic, a macrolide (azithromycin) or doxycycline.

micro-lab-id.title: Laboratory identification of IE organisms
points: S. aureus: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; golden yellow colonies, beta hemolysis, ferments mannitol; catalase and coagulase positive.
S. epidermidis: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive, coagulase negative.
Viridans streptococci (S. mutans): Gram-positive cocci in chains; alpha hemolysis; optochin resistant; insoluble in bile.
S. pyogenes: Gram-positive cocci in chains; beta hemolysis; catalase negative.
S. pneumoniae: lancet-shaped capsulated diplococci; alpha hemolysis; optochin sensitive; bile soluble.

emb-arches.title: Formation and derivatives of the aortic arches
points: At the 4th week two primitive aortae appear, each with a ventral aorta, a dorsal aorta and a connecting segment; the ventral aortae fuse into the aortic sac with right and left horns.
1st arch: disappears, remnant forms the maxillary arteries. 2nd arch: disappears, remnant forms the stapedial arteries. 5th arch: disappears completely.
3rd arch: proximal parts form the common carotid arteries; distal parts join the dorsal aorta to form the internal carotid arteries. The external carotid is a new bud from the junction.
Left 4th arch: part of the arch of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian. Right 4th arch: proximal part of the right subclavian artery.
6th arch: left proximal forms the left pulmonary artery and left distal forms the ductus arteriosus; right proximal forms the right pulmonary artery and right distal degenerates.

emb-sac-dorsal.title: Aortic sac, dorsal aorta and the origin of the great arteries
points: Aortic sac: arch of the aorta proximal to the brachiocephalic artery. Left horn: arch between the brachiocephalic and left common carotid. Right horn: brachiocephalic artery.
Right dorsal aorta: cranial to the 3rd arch forms the distal internal carotid; at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the distal right subclavian; the rest degenerates.

Left dorsal aorta: at the 7th intersegmental artery forms the subclavian; between the 4th and 6th arches forms the distal arch of the aorta; caudal to the 6th arch forms the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta.
Arch of the aorta from proximal to distal: aortic sac, left horn, left 4th arch, left dorsal aorta between the 4th and 6th arches.

emb-anomalies.title: Anomalies of the aortic arches
points: Patent ductus arteriosus: a patent duct between the left pulmonary artery and the arch of the aorta; associated with aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis and Fallot's tetralogy.
Right arch of aorta: develops from the right dorsal aorta and right 4th arch.
Double arch of aorta: persistence of the distal right dorsal aorta; a vascular ring around the trachea (dyspnea) and esophagus (dysphagia).
Coarctation: constriction of the aorta distal to the left subclavian. Postductal: distal to the ductus, ductus usually closed. Preductal: proximal to the ductus, ductus open.

emb-veins.title: Development of the veins
points: At the 5th week each horn of the sinus venosus receives the umbilical, vitelline and common cardinal veins.
Vitelline veins form the portal and superior mesenteric veins. After birth the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum and the left umbilical vein the ligamentum teres.
Right common cardinal vein: SVC inside the pericardium. Left common cardinal vein: oblique vein of the left atrium.

Right anterior cardinal: SVC outside the pericardium, right brachiocephalic and right internal jugular veins. Left anterior cardinal: left superior intercostal, left brachiocephalic and left internal jugular veins.
Posterior cardinal veins: IVC, common iliac, suprarenal, testicular or ovarian, and renal veins.
